long_notes.Electric Potential and Potential Differe:
Electric Potential ($V$) – work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to a point in an electric field.

Mathematically, $V = \frac{W}{q}$ where $W$ is work (J) and $q$ is charge (C). SI unit: volt (V) = J·C$^{-1}$.

Potential Difference ($\Delta V$) – difference of potentials between two points: $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = \frac{W_{AB}}{q}$.

  • For a uniform electric field $E$, $\Delta V = -E d$ ( $d$ = separation along field).
  • Relation with electric field: $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$ (in 1‑D, $E = -\frac{dV}{dx}$).

Derivation of potential of a point charge

Work to bring $q$ from $\infty$ to distance $r$ from charge $Q$: $W = \int_{\infty}^{r} \frac{k Q q}{r'^2} dr' = k \frac{Q q}{r}$. Hence $V(r) = \frac{W}{q} = k \frac{Q}{r}$, where $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Electric Potential$V$$V = \frac{W}{q}$volt (V)
Potential Difference$\Delta V$$\Delta V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$volt (V)
Potential of point charge$V$$V = k \frac{Q}{r}$volt (V)

Example

Find the potential at a point 5 cm from a charge $Q = 2\,\mu\text{C}$.

Solution: $V = k \frac{Q}{r} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\times10^{-6}}{0.05} \approx 3.6\times10^{4}\,\text{V}$.
long_notes.Equipotential Surfaces:
Definition: An equipotential surface is a locus of points in space that have the same electric potential, i.e., $V=\text{constant}$. No work is done in moving a test charge $q$ anywhere on this surface because $\Delta V=0$.

Key properties

  • All points are at the same potential; $\Delta V=0$ between any two points on the surface.
  • The electric field $\mathbf{E}$ is always perpendicular to the surface: $\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=0$ for any displacement $d\mathbf{l}$ lying on the surface.
  • Equipotential surfaces never intersect.
  • Closer surfaces indicate a stronger field magnitude $|\mathbf{E}|=|\nabla V|$.

Fundamental relation

The potential difference between two points $i$ and $f$ is given by $$\Delta V = -\int_{i}^{f}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l}$$ and for a radial field of a point charge $Q$, the potential at distance $r$ is $$V(r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$$ leading \to spherical equipotentials.

SI unit: volt (V) where $1\,\text{V}=1\,\text{J\,C}^{-1}$.

Example

Find the work done \in moving a charge $q=2\,\mu\text{C}$ from $r_{A}=0.10\,\text{m}$ \to $r_{B}=0.20\,\text{m}$ \in the field of a point charge $Q=5\,\mu\text{C}$.

Potential at $r$ is $V(r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$. Hence

StepExpression
1$\Delta V = V_{B}-V_{A}=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}Q\left(\frac{1}{r_{B}}-\frac{1}{r_{A}}\right)$
2Insert values: $\Delta V = 9\times10^{9}\times5\times10^{-6}\left(\frac{1}{0.20}-\frac{1}{0.10}\right)\,\text{V}= -2.25\times10^{5}\,\text{V}$
3Work $W = q\Delta V = 2\times10^{-6}\times(-2.25\times10^{5})\,\text{J}= -0.45\,\text{J}$

The negative sign indicates that the external agent must do $0.45\,\text{J}$ of work against the attractive field.
long_notes.Potential due to Point Charge and System:
Definition: Electric potential $V$ at a point is the work done by external agent in bringing a unit positive test charge from infinity to that point without acceleration.

Formula for a point charge: $$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}$$ where $q$ is the source charge, $r$ the distance from it and $\varepsilon_0$ the permittivity of free space. SI unit: volt (V) = J/C.

Potential due \to a system of point charges (superposition): $$V = \sum_{i}\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_i}{r_i}$$

Relation with electric field: $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$; for radial fields $E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ and the potential difference between points A and B is $\Delta V = -\int_{A}^{B}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$.

SymbolQuantitySI Unit
$V$Electric potential$V$ (volt)
$q$Charge$C$ (coulomb)
$r$Distance from charge$m$ (metre)
$\varepsilon_0$Permittivity of free space$F\,m^{-1}$

Solved Example:

  • Two point charges $q_1=+2\,\mu C$ and $q_2=-3\,\mu C$ are placed $0.20\,m$ apart on a straight line.
  • Find the potential at point $P$ which lies $0.10\,m$ from $q_1$ on the line joining the charges.

Distances: $r_1=0.10\,m$, $r_2=0.20-0.10=0.10\,m$. Using superposition,

$$V_P = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_1}{r_1}+\frac{q_2}{r_2}\right)$$

Substituting $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\,N\,m^{2}C^{-2}$, $q_1=2\times10^{-6}\,C$, $q_2=-3\times10^{-6}\,C$, $r_1=r_2=0.10\,m$,

$$V_P = 9\times10^{9}\left(\frac{2\times10^{-6}}{0.10}+\frac{-3\times10^{-6}}{0.10}\right)$$

$$V_P = 9\times10^{9}\left(2\times10^{-5}-3\times10^{-5}\right) = 9\times10^{9}(-1\times10^{-5}) = -9\times10^{4}\,V$$

Thus the potential at $P$ is $-9\times10^{4}\,\text{V}$ (negative because the larger magnitude charge is negative).
long_notes.Relation between Electric Field and Pote:
Definition: The electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point is the force experienced per unit positive test charge, while the potential gradient is the spatial rate of change of the electric potential $V$.

Fundamental relation (vector form):

$\vec{E}= -\nabla V$

In one‑dimensional motion along $x$:

$E_{x}= -\frac{dV}{dx}$

  • Negative sign indicates that the field points from higher to lower potential.
  • For a uniform field, $E$ is constant and $V$ varies linearly with distance.
FormulaSI Unit
$\vec{E}= -\nabla V$$\text{V m}^{-1}$
$E= -\frac{dV}{dx}$$\text{V m}^{-1}$

Derivation (brief): Work done in moving a charge $q$ through a potential difference $dV$ is $dW = q\,dV$. By definition $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}= q\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}$. Equating and dividing by $q\,ds$ gives $\vec{E}\cdot \hat{s}= -\frac{dV}{ds}$, leading to $\vec{E}= -\nabla V$.

Example: Two parallel plates are 4 cm apart and maintain a potential difference of 200 V. Find the magnitude and direction of $\vec{E}$ between the plates.

Solution:

$d = 4\,\text{cm}=0.04\,\text{m}$

$E = -\frac{\Delta V}{d}= -\frac{200\,\text{V}}{0.04\,\text{m}} = -5.0\times10^{3}\,\text{V m}^{-1}$.

The magnitude is $5.0\times10^{3}\,\text{V m}^{-1}$ and the field points from the positive plate toward the negative plate.
long_notes.Capacitance: Definition and Units:
Definition: Capacitance ($C$) of a conductor is the ability to store electric charge per unit potential difference. It is defined as $C = \\frac{Q}{V}$ where $Q$ is the charge on the conductor and $V$ is the potential difference between the conductor and a reference point.

SI unit: The SI unit of capacitance is the farad (F), where $1\\,\\text{F}=\\frac{\\text{Coulomb}}{\\text{Volt}}$.

  • Symbol: $C$
  • Dimension: $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^{4}I^{2}]$
  • Common multiples: $1\\,\\mu\\text{F}=10^{-6}\\,\\text{F}$, $1\\,\\text{nF}=10^{-9}\\,\\text{F}$, $1\\,\\text{pF}=10^{-12}\\,\\text{F}$

Parallel‑plate capacitor: For two parallel plates of area $A$ separated by distance $d$ (air or vacuum between them), the capacitance is

$$C = \\varepsilon_{0}\\,\\frac{A}{d}$$

where $\\varepsilon_{0}=8.85\\times10^{-12}\\,\\text{F·m}^{-1}$ is the permittivity of free space.

QuantitySymbolSI Unit
Capacitance$C$farad (F)
Charge$Q$coulomb (C)
Potential difference$V$volt (V)

Solved example:

Find the capacitance of a parallel‑plate capacitor with plate area $A = 2\\,\\text{cm}^{2}$ and separation $d = 0.5\\,\\text{mm}$ (air gap).

Solution:

  1. Convert \to SI units: $A = 2\\times10^{-4}\\,\\text{m}^{2}$, $d = 5\\times10^{-4}\\,\\text{m}$.
  2. Use $C = \\varepsilon_{0}\\,\\frac{A}{d}$.
  3. $$C = 8.85\\times10^{-12}\\,\\frac{2\\times10^{-4}}{5\\times10^{-4}} = 8.85\\times10^{-12}\\times0.4 = 3.54\\times10^{-12}\\,\\text{F}$$
  4. Thus $C \\approx 3.5\\,\\text{pF}$.
long_notes.Combination of Capacitors:
Definition: A capacitor stores electric charge $Q$ at a potential difference $V$. Its capacitance $C$ is defined as $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ (SI unit: farad, F).

Combination of Capacitors

  • Series connection: The same charge $Q$ flows through each capacitor, while the total voltage is the sum of individual voltages. Equivalent capacitance $$C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{\sum \frac{1}{C_i}}$$ or for two capacitors $C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$.
  • Parallel connection: The voltage across each capacitor is identical, and the total charge is the \sum of individual charges. Equivalent capacitance $$C_{\text{eq}} = \sum C_i$$ or for two capacitors $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2$$.
ConnectionFormula for $C_{\text{eq}}$Voltage distributionCharge distribution
Series$\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}}=\sum \frac{1}{C_i}$$V_{\text{total}}=\sum V_i$$Q$ same on each
Parallel$C_{\text{eq}}=\sum C_i$$V$ same on each$Q_i = C_i V$

Example: Two capacitors $C_1 = 4\,\mu\text{F}$ and $C_2 = 6\,\mu\text{F}$ are connected \in series across a $12\,\text{V}$ battery.

  1. Equivalent capacitance: $C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}=\frac{4\times6}{4+6}=\frac{24}{10}=2.4\,\mu\text{F}$.
  2. Charge on the series combination: $Q = C_{\text{eq}} V = 2.4\times10^{-6}\times12 = 28.8\times10^{-6}\,\text{C}$.
  3. Voltage across each: $V_1 = \frac{Q}{C_1}=\frac{28.8\times10^{-6}}{4\times10^{-6}}=7.2\,\text{V}$, $V_2 = 12-7.2 = 4.8\,\text{V}$.

Key points: In series, $C_{\text{eq}}$ is always less than the smallest individual capacitor; \in parallel, $C_{\text{eq}}$ is the arithmetic sum.
long_notes.Energy Stored in Capacitors:
Definition: Energy stored in a capacitor is the work done in moving charge from one plate to the other while charging.

Derivation:

  • At an instant the potential difference is $V = \frac{q}{C}$.
  • Incremental work $dW = V\,dq = \frac{q}{C}\,dq$.
  • Integrating from $0$ to $Q$: $W = \int_0^{Q} \frac{q}{C}\,dq = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{C}$.

Hence the energy $U$ can be written in three equivalent forms:

FormExpression
$U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$useful when $C$ and $V$ are known
$U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$useful when $Q$ and $C$ are known
$U = \frac{1}{2} Q V$general form

SI Unit: Joule (J). $[C] = \mathrm{F}$, $[V] = \mathrm{V}$.

Energy density in a uniform electric field: $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$ (J\,m$^{-3}$).

Example: A $10\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged to $200\,$V. Find the stored energy.

  1. Convert capacitance: $C = 10\times10^{-6}\,\text{F}$.
  2. Apply $U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$:
  3. $U = 0.5 \times 10\times10^{-6} \times 200^2 = 0.5 \times 10\times10^{-6} \times 40000 = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2\,\text{J}$.

Thus the capacitor stores $0.2\,$J of energy.
long_notes.Capacitors with Dielectrics and Spherica:
Dielectric in a Capacitor

  • Definition: A dielectric is an insulating material that, when placed between the plates of a capacitor, reduces the effective electric field.
  • Dielectric constant $k$ (or relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$) is defined as $k = \frac{C_{\text{with dielectric}}}{C_{\text{vacuum}}}$ (unitless).
  • Capacitance with dielectric: $C = k\,\epsilon_0 \frac{A}{d}$, where $A$ (m$^2$) is plate area, $d$ (m) separation, $\epsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F·m$^{-1}$.
  • Maximum voltage: $V_{\max} = \frac{E_{\text{break}} d}{k}$, $E_{\text{break}}$ is dielectric strength (V·m$^{-1}$).

Spherical Capacitor

  • Two concentric spherical conductors of radii $a$ (inner) and $b$ (outer, $b>a$).
  • Capacitance in vacuum: $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 \frac{ab}{b-a}$.
  • With dielectric filling the region $a
  • Energy stored: $U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$.
QuantitySymbolSI Unit
Capacitance$C$farad (F)
Dielectric constant$k$unitless
Permittivity of free space$\epsilon_0$F·m$^{-1}$
Charge$Q$coulomb (C)
Potential difference$V$volt (V)

Example

Find the capacitance of a spherical capacitor with $a=2\,$cm, $b=5\,$cm when the space between the spheres is filled with a dielectric of $k=2.5$.

Solution:

Using $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 k \frac{ab}{b-a}$, convert \to metres: $a=0.02\,$m, $b=0.05\,$m.

$C = 4\pi (8.85\times10^{-12}) (2.5) \frac{0.02\times0.05}{0.05-0.02}$

$= 4\pi (8.85\times10^{-12}) (2.5) \frac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{0.03}$

$\approx 4\pi (8.85\times10^{-12}) (2.5) (3.33\times10^{-2})$

$\approx 9.2\times10^{-12}\,\text{F}$ (≈9.2 pF).

short_notes.title: Important Formulas
short_notes.html:
FormulaDescription
$\displaystyle V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}$Potential at a distance $r$ from a point charge $q$.
$\displaystyle \Delta V = -\int_{a}^{b}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$Potential difference between points $a$ and $b$.
$\displaystyle C = \frac{Q}{V}$Definition of capacitance.
$\displaystyle C = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$Capacitance of a parallel‑plate capacitor (vacuum).
$\displaystyle C = \kappa C_0 = \kappa\frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$Capacitance with a dielectric of constant $\kappa$.
$\displaystyle U = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}$Energy stored in a capacitor.
$\displaystyle \frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \sum_{i}\frac{1}{C_i}$Series combination of capacitors.
$\displaystyle C_{eq}=\sum_{i}C_i$Parallel combination of capacitors.
$\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d}$Uniform electric field between parallel plates.
$\displaystyle u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^{2}$Energy density of the electric field in vacuum.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Electric Potential (V): Work done per unit positive charge to bring it from infinity to a point, $V = \frac{W}{q}$.
  • Potential Difference (\Delta V): Difference in electric potential between two points; equals the work done per unit charge in moving between them.
  • Capacitance (C): Ability of a system to store charge per unit potential, $C = \frac{Q}{V}$.
  • Dielectric Constant (\kappa): Ratio of capacitance with dielectric to that without, $\kappa = \frac{C}{C_0}=\frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon_0}$.
  • Energy Stored (U): $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}$.
  • Electric Field between Plates: $E = \frac{V}{d}$ (uniform for ideal parallel plates).

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
• Always write $\epsilon_0$ for vacuum; replace with $\epsilon = \kappa\epsilon_0$ only when a dielectric fills the capacitor.
• Sign convention: potential decreases in the direction of the electric field, hence $\Delta V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$.
• For series capacitors use the reciprocal sum; for parallel, add directly.
• Edge effects are ignored in the parallel‑plate formula $C = \epsilon_0 A/d$; this is valid only when $d \ll \sqrt{A}$.
• Energy density formula $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^{2}$ applies to vacuum; with a dielectric use $\epsilon$ instead of $\epsilon_0$.
• Do not confuse $V$ (potential) with $\Delta V$ (potential difference) – the former is a scalar at a point, the latter is the difference between two points.

long_notes.Electric current, potential difference a:
Electric current, potential difference and emf

These three concepts form the basis of circuit analysis. They are defined precisely and related through simple algebraic expressions.

  • Electric current ($I$): rate of flow of charge, $I=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$, SI unit – ampere (A).
  • Potential difference ($V$): work done per unit charge, $V=\frac{W}{Q}$, SI unit – volt (V).
  • Electromotive force ($\varepsilon$): work done by a source per unit charge while moving charge from its negative to positive terminal, $\varepsilon=\frac{W_{\text{source}}}{Q}$, SI unit – volt (V).

Key formulas

  • Ohm’s law: $V=IR$.
  • Resistance of a uniform conductor: $R=\rho\frac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is resistivity, $l$ length, $A$ cross‑section.
  • Drift velocity: $v_{d}=\frac{I}{nAe}$, $n$ – charge carrier density, $e$ – elementary charge.
  • Power: $P=VI=I^{2}R=\frac{V^{2}}{R}$.
  • Terminal potential of a cell with internal resistance $r$: $V=\varepsilon- Ir$.

Symbols and SI units

SymbolQuantitySI unit
$I$CurrentA
$V$Potential differenceV
$\varepsilon$EMFV
$R$Resistance\Omega
$r$Internal resistance\Omega

Solved example

A cell of emf $\varepsilon=12\,\text{V}$ has internal resistance $r=0.5\,\Omega$. It is connected to an external resistor $R=4\,\Omega$. Find (i) the current $I$ and (ii) the terminal voltage $V$ across the external resistor.

Solution:

  1. Total resistance $R_{\text{tot}}=R+r=4+0.5=4.5\,\Omega$.
  2. Current $I=\frac{\varepsilon}{R_{\text{tot}}}=\frac{12}{4.5}=2.67\,\text{A}$.
  3. Terminal voltage $V=\varepsilon- Ir=12-(2.67)(0.5)=10.67\,\text{V}$.

The result shows how internal resistance reduces the voltage available to the external circuit.
long_notes.Ohm’s law and resistance:
Ohm’s Law – For a conductor kept at constant temperature, the potential difference $V$ across it is directly proportional to the current $I$ flowing through it.

Mathematically, $V = I R$ where $R$ is the resistance (constant for a given material and geometry).

  • Resistance $R = \rho \frac{l}{A}$, $\rho$ = resistivity, $l$ = length, $A$ = cross‑sectional area.
  • SI unit of $R$ is $\Omega$ (ohm), of $\rho$ is $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$.
  • From Ohm’s law, $R = \frac{V}{I}$.
  • Temperature effect: $R = R_0[1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$, $\alpha$ = temperature coefficient.
  • Electrical power: $P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}$.
SymbolQuantitySI Unit
$V$Potential difference$\text{volt (V)}$
$I$Current$\text{ampere (A)}$
$R$Resistance$\Omega$
$\rho$Resistivity$\Omega\cdot\text{m}$

Example

Find the current through a copper wire of length $l = 2\,$m, cross‑section $A = 1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2$, resistivity $\rho = 1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$, when a voltage $V = 12\,$V is applied.

Resistance $R = \rho \frac{l}{A} = 1.68\times10^{-8}\times\frac{2}{1.0\times10^{-6}} = 0.0336\,\Omega$.

Current $I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{0.0336} \approx 357\,\text{A}$.
long_notes.Resistivity and temperature coefficient:
Resistivity ($\rho$) – intrinsic property of a material that relates its resistance to its dimensions. It is defined as the resistance of a cube of side 1 m. SI unit: $\Omega\,m$.

Temperature coefficient of resistance ($\alpha$) – fractional change in resistance per degree Celsius at a reference temperature (usually $20\,^{\circ}\!C$). SI unit: $\text{K}^{-1}$.

  • Resistance of a uniform conductor: $R = \rho\,\frac{L}{A}$ where $L$ is length (m) and $A$ is cross‑sectional area (m$^2$).
  • Variation of resistivity with temperature: $\rho_T = \rho_0\,[1+\alpha\,(T- T_0)]$.
  • Corresponding variation of resistance: $R_T = R_0\,[1+\alpha\,(T- T_0)]$.
SymbolQuantitySI Unit
$\rho$Resistivity$\Omega\,m$
$R$Resistance$\Omega$
$\alpha$Temperature coefficient of resistance$\text{K}^{-1}$
$L$Length of conductorm
$A$Cross‑sectional aream$^2$

Example: A copper wire of length $L=2\,\text{m}$ and cross‑section $A=0.5\,\text{mm}^2$ is at $20\,^{\circ}\!C$. Given $\rho_{20}=1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,m$, find its resistance.

Convert area: $A = 0.5\,\text{mm}^2 = 0.5\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2 = 5\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2$.

Use $R = \rho\,\frac{L}{A}$:

$$R = (1.68\times10^{-8})\,\frac{2}{5\times10^{-7}} = (1.68\times10^{-8})\times4\times10^{6}=6.72\times10^{-2}\,\Omega$$

Thus, $R \approx 0.067\,\Omega$ at $20\,^{\circ}\!C$. If the temperature rises \to $50\,^{\circ}\!C$ and $\alpha_{Cu}=3.9\times10^{-3}\,\text{K}^{-1}$, then $R_{50}=R_{20}[1+\alpha(50-20)] = 0.067[1+3.9\times10^{-3}\times30]\approx 0.069\,\Omega$.
long_notes.Series and parallel combinations of resi:
Definition: A combination of resistors is called series when the same current flows through each resistor one after another, and parallel when the terminals of all resistors are connected together so that the voltage across each resistor is identical.

SI unit of resistance: ohm, $\Omega$.

Series combination

  • Equivalent resistance: $R_{\text{eq}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_i$.
  • Current through each resistor is the same: $I$.
  • Voltage across the combination: $V=I\,R_{\text{eq}}$.

Parallel combination

  • Reciprocal of equivalent resistance: $\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_i}$.
  • Voltage across each resistor is the same: $V$.
  • Current through each resistor: $I_i=\frac{V}{R_i}$, total current $I=\sum I_i$.

Derivation for two resistors

Series: $R_{\text{eq}}=R_1+R_2$ follows directly from $V=V_1+V_2=I(R_1+R_2)$. Parallel: $\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}}=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}$ is obtained from $I=I_1+I_2=\frac{V}{R_1}+\frac{V}{R_2}=V\left(\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$, thus $I=\frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}}$.

Example (Solved)

Find the equivalent resistance of three resistors $R_1=10\,\Omega$, $R_2=20\,\Omega$, $R_3=30\,\Omega$:

  1. Series: $R_{\text{eq(series)}}=10+20+30=60\,\Omega$.
  2. Parallel: \[\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq(par)}}}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{30}=\frac{6+3+2}{60}=\frac{11}{60}\] Hence $R_{\text{eq(par)}}=\frac{60}{11}\approx5.45\,\Omega$.

These results are frequently used in circuit analysis and exam problems.
long_notes.Kirchhoff’s laws (junction and loop rule:
Kirchhoff’s Junction (Current) Rule

  • At any junction, the algebraic sum of currents is zero: $$\\sum I_{\\text{\in}} = \\sum I_{\\text{out}}$$ or $$\\sum I = 0$$.
  • SI unit of current: $A$ (ampere).

Kirchhoff’s Loop (Voltage) Rule

  • For any closed loop, the algebraic \sum of potential differences equals zero: $$\\sum V = 0$$ or $$\\sum I R = 0$$.
  • Potential rise is taken positive, drop negative.
  • SI unit of voltage: $V$ (volt).

Derivation (Brief)

  • Junction rule follows from charge conservation: no charge accumulation at a node.
  • Loop rule follows from energy conservation: work done by emf equals \sum of $IR$ drops.

Key Formulas

ExpressionMeaning
$$\\sum I = 0$$Current conservation at a node
$$\\sum V = 0$$Voltage conservation \in a loop
$$V = IR$$Ohm’s law ( $V$ \in $V$, $I$ \in $A$, $R$ \in $\\Omega$ )

Example

In the circuit below, find the unknown current $I_2$ (all resistances \in $\\Omega$, emf \in $V$):

ComponentValue
$\\mathcal{E}_1$$12$
$R_1$$4$
$R_2$$6$
$\\mathcal{E}_2$$6$

Applying KCL at the junction: $$I_1 = I_2 + I_3$$.

Loop 1 (\left): $$\\mathcal{E}_1 - I_1R_1 - I_2R_2 = 0$$.

Loop 2 (\right): $$\\mathcal{E}_2 - I_3R_2 = 0$$.

Solving, $I_3 = \frac{\\mathcal{E}_2}{R_2}=1\ \text{A}$, $I_1 = \frac{\\mathcal{E}_1}{R_1}=3\ \text{A}$, thus $I_2 = I_1 - I_3 = 2\ \text{A}$.

Result: $I_2 = 2\ \text{A}$ (direction from $R_2$ to the junction).
long_notes.Wheatstone bridge and its applications:
Definition: A Wheatstone bridge is a network of four resistors $R_1,R_2,R_3,R_x$ forming a diamond with a galvanometer between the two opposite nodes.

Balance condition: When the bridge is balanced (no current through galvanometer) the ratio of resistances in one branch equals that in the other branch:

BranchRatio
$R_1$ : $R_2$$=$
$R_3$ : $R_x$$=$

Mathematically, $$\frac{R_1}{R_2}=\frac{R_3}{R_x}$$ leading \to $$R_x=\frac{R_2 R_3}{R_1}$$ (SI unit: $\Omega$).

Derivation (brief):

  • Apply Kirchhoff’s voltage law \to the two loops.
  • Set galvanometer current $I_g=0$ at balance.
  • Equate the potential drops $I_1R_1=I_3R_3$ and $I_2R_2=I_xR_x$.
  • Eliminate currents \to obtain the ratio above.

Key applications:

  • Precise measurement of an unknown resistance.
  • Sensor for strain, temperature (using a strain gauge as $R_x$).
  • Calibration of resistance standards.

Example: In a balanced bridge $R_1=100\,\Omega$, $R_2=200\,\Omega$, $R_3=150\,\Omega$. Find $R_x$.

Solution:

  1. Use $R_x=\frac{R_2 R_3}{R_1}$.
  2. Substitute: $R_x=\frac{200\times150}{100}=300\,\Omega$.
  3. Thus the unknown resistance is $300\,\Omega$.
long_notes.Potentiometer and measurement of emf:
Definition: A potentiometer is a device that compares an unknown emf with a known potential difference by using a uniform potential gradient along a calibrated wire, giving a null deflection of the galvanometer.

Principle: When a constant current $I$ flows through a uniform wire of length $l$, the potential drop is $V$, producing a constant potential gradient $K = \frac{V}{l}$ (V m$^{-1}$). At the balance point the unknown emf $e$ equals the potential difference across the balanced length $l_1$: $e = K l_1$.

  • Potential gradient $K$ (SI unit V m$^{-1}$)
  • Balance length $l_1$ (m)
  • Unknown emf $e$ (V)
SymbolQuantityUnit
$K$Potential gradientV m$^{-1}$
$l$Total length of wirem
$l_1$Balance lengthm
$e$Emf of cellV

Derivation of emf: With a known current $I$, the total drop $V = I R_{wire}$ across the whole wire of length $l$ gives $K = \frac{I R_{wire}}{l}$. At balance, $e = K l_1 = \frac{I R_{wire}}{l}\, l_1$.

Example: A potentiometer wire of length $1.0\,\text{m}$ carries a current such that $K = 2.0\,\text{V m}^{-1}$. The galvanometer shows null when the balance length is $0.45\,\text{m}$. Find the emf of the cell.

Solution:
$e = K l_1 = 2.0 \times 0.45 = 0.90\,\text{V}$.

Thus the cell’s emf is $0.90\,\text{V}$.

long_notes.Magnetic field and its properties:
Magnetic Field (B) – A vector field that exerts a magnetic force on moving charges. Direction given by right‑hand rule; SI unit is tesla (T) = $\frac{N}{A\,m}$.

Key Properties

  • Field lines are continuous; they emerge from north pole and enter south pole.
  • Magnitude at a distance $r$ from a long straight conductor carrying current $I$: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
  • For a solenoid (n turns per unit length, length $l$): $B = \mu_0 n I$ (inside, neglecting edge effects).

Force on a Moving Charge

Lorentz force: $\vec{F} = q\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$. Magnitude $F = qvB\sin\theta$ where $\theta$ is angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$.

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Magnetic field$B$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$tesla (T)
Force on charge$F$$F = qvB\sin\theta$newton (N)
Force on current element$d\vec{F}$$d\vec{F}= I\,d\vec{l}\times\vec{B}$newton (N)

Sample Problem

A proton (charge $q = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$) moves with speed $v = 2\times10^{6}\,\text{m/s}$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.5\,\text{T}$. Find the magnetic force on the proton.

Solution: Since $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, $\sin\theta = 1$.

$F = qvB = (1.6\times10^{-19})(2\times10^{6})(0.5) = 1.6\times10^{-13}\,\text{N}$.

Direction is given by right‑hand rule (out of the page for a positive charge).
long_notes.Motion of charged particles in uniform m:
Uniform magnetic field: A magnetic field of constant magnitude and direction throughout the region.

Lorentz force on a moving charge: $\mathbf{F}=q\,\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, magnitude $F=qvB\sin\theta$.

When $\theta=90^{\circ}$ the particle moves in a circle. Equating magnetic force to centripetal force $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ gives

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

Period and frequency are

$$T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB},\qquad f=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$

SI units: $q$ (C), $v$ (m·s$^{-1}$), $B$ (T), $m$ (kg), $r$ (m), $T$ (s), $f$ (Hz).

QuantityFormulaUnit
Radius $r$$\frac{mv}{qB}$m
Period $T$$\frac{2\pi m}{qB}$s
Frequency $f$$\frac{qB}{2\pi m}$Hz

Example: A proton ($q=+1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, $m=1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg) enters a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5$ T perpendicular \to its velocity $v=2.0\times10^{6}$ m·s$^{-1}$. Find $r$ and $T$.

Radius:

$$r=\frac{(1.67\times10^{-27})(2.0\times10^{6})}{(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.5)}=2.09\times10^{-2}\,\text{m}$$

Period:

$$T=\frac{2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})}{(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.5)}=1.31\times10^{-7}\,\text{s}$$
long_notes.Force on a current-carrying conductor an:
Force on a current‑carrying conductor

  • Definition: The magnetic force experienced by a straight conductor of length $\\ell$ carrying current $I$ placed in a uniform magnetic field $\\vec B$ is $\\vec F = I\\,\\vec \ell \times \\vec B$.
  • SI unit: Newton (N). $I$ in ampere (A), $\\ell$ in metre (m), $B$ in tesla (T).
  • Derivation: Consider a charge $q$ moving with drift velocity $\\vec v_d$; force on each charge $q\\vec v_d \times \\vec B$. Number of charges per unit length $nA$, total force $F = (nA\\,\\ell) q\\,\\vec v_d \times \\vec B = I\\,\\vec \ell \times \\vec B$ because $I = nqA v_d$.

Hall effect

  • Definition: Development of a transverse electric field $\\vec E_H$ across a conductor when a magnetic field $\\vec B$ is applied perpendicular to the direction of current.
  • Hall coefficient: $R_H = \frac{E_H}{J B}=\frac{1}{n e}$, where $n$ is carrier density and $e$ the elementary charge.
  • Hall voltage: $V_H = R_H \frac{I B}{t}$ for a slab of thickness $t$.
  • SI unit: Volt (V) for $V_H$, tesla (T) for $B$.

Example

A rectangular copper strip (width $w=2\,\text{cm}$, thickness $t=0.5\,\text{mm}$) carries $I=5\,\text{A}$ and is placed in a uniform $B=0.2\,\text{T}$ field perpendicular to the strip. Find the Hall voltage.

Solution: $R_H = \frac{1}{n e}$ for Cu, $n \approx 8.5\times10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$, so $R_H \approx 7.35\times10^{-11}\,\text{m}^3\text{C}^{-1}$. $V_H = R_H \frac{I B}{t}=7.35\times10^{-11}\times\frac{5\times0.2}{5\times10^{-4}} \approx 1.47\times10^{-5}\,\text{V}$ (≈15 µV).
long_notes.Torque on a current loop and magnetic di:
Definition: The torque $\vec{\tau}$ on a planar current loop of area $A$ carrying current $I$ placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by
$\vec{\tau}=\vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}$, where the magnetic dipole moment $\vec{\mu}=I\vec{A}$ (direction normal to the loop by the right‑hand rule).

Key derivation:

  • Consider a rectangular loop of sides $l$ and $w$ (area $A=l w$). The forces on opposite sides are $F_{1}=I l B\sin\theta$ and $F_{2}=I w B\sin\theta$ acting at distances $w/2$ and $l/2$ from the centre.
  • The net torque about the centre is $\tau=IAB\sin\theta$.
  • Writing $\mu=IA$, the compact vector form becomes $\vec{\tau}=\vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}$.

SI units:

QuantitySymbolUnit
Current$I$A
Area$A$m$^{2}$
Magnetic field$B$T (kg·s$^{-2}$·A$^{-1}$)
Magnetic dipole moment$\mu$A·m$^{2}$
Torque$\tau$N·m

Example (solved): A square loop of side $0.10\,\text{m}$ carries $I=5\,\text{A}$. It is placed in a uniform field $B=0.20\,\text{T}$ making an angle $\theta=30^{\circ}$ with the normal to the loop. Find the torque.

  • Area $A=(0.10)^{2}=0.010\,\text{m}^{2}$.
  • Magnetic dipole moment $\mu=IA=5\times0.010=0.050\,\text{A·m}^{2}$.
  • Torque $\tau=\mu B\sin\theta=0.050\times0.20\times\sin30^{\circ}=0.050\times0.20\times0.5=0.005\,\text{N·m}$.

Thus the loop experiences a torque of $5\times10^{-3}\,\text{N·m}$, tending to align its magnetic moment with the external field.
long_notes.Biot–Savart law and magnetic field due t:
Biot–Savart Law: The magnetic field $d\vec{B}$ produced at a point P by an infinitesimal element $d\vec{l}$ of a current‑carrying conductor is given by
$d\vec{B}= \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l}\times \hat{r}}{r^2}$, where $I$ is the current (A), $\hat{r}$ is the unit vector from $d\vec{l}$ to P, $r$ is the distance (m) and $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T·m/A}$.

Magnetic field of a long straight conductor (infinite length):
Integrating the Biot–Savart expression over the whole wire gives
$B= \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, directed azimuthally according to the right‑hand rule. SI unit: tesla (T).

Key symbols:

SymbolQuantitySI unit
$I$CurrentA
$r$Radial distance from wirem
$\mu_0$Permeability of free spaceT·m/A
$B$Magnetic field strengthT

Example:

  • Find $B$ at a point 5 cm from a long straight wire carrying $I=3\,\text{A}$.

Using $B= \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$,
$B= \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3}{2\pi\times0.05}= \frac{12\pi\times10^{-7}}{0.1\pi}=1.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}=12\,\mu\text{T}$.

Thus the magnetic field 5 cm away is $12\,\mu\text{T}$, directed clockwise when the current flows away from the observer.
long_notes.Ampère’s circuital law:
Definition: Ampère’s circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ around a closed path equals $\mu_0$ times the net current $I_{\text{enc}}$ threading the surface bounded by the path.

Mathematically, $$\oint_{\text{C}} \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=\mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}$$ where $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{H\,m}^{-1}$.

  • Applicable only when the path is chosen such that $\mathbf{B}$ is either constant \in magnitude or perpendicular \to $d\mathbf{l}$.
  • For highly symmetric situations (infinite straight wire, solenoid, toroid) the law yields simple expressions for $\mathbf{B}$.

Key derivation – infinite straight conductor: Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ coaxial with the wire. $\mathbf{B}$ is tangential and has constant magnitude on the loop, and $d\mathbf{l}$ is along the tangent, so $\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=B\,dl$. Hence $$\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=B(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I$$ giving $$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$

SymbolQuantitySI Unit
$\mu_0$Permeability of free spaceH·m$^{-1}$
$I$CurrentA
$r$Radial distance from wirem
$B$Magnetic fieldT

Example: Find $B$ at a distance $r=5\,\text{cm}$ from a long straight wire carrying $I=3\,\text{A}$.

Using $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, $$B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3}{2\pi\times0.05}=\frac{12\pi\times10^{-7}}{0.1\pi}=1.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$$

Thus the magnetic field 5 cm away is $1.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$ directed azimuthally according to the right‑hand rule.
long_notes.Earth’s magnetic field and magnetic dipo:
Earth’s Magnetic Field and Magnetic Dipole

The Earth behaves like a gigantic bar magnet whose magnetic axis is inclined to the geographic axis. The field produced is called the Earth’s magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}$) and is approximated by the field of a magnetic dipole placed at the centre of the Earth.

Magnetic dipole moment ($\mathbf{m}$) of a current loop is defined as $\mathbf{m}=I\,\mathbf{A}$, where $I$ is the current and $\mathbf{A}$ is the vector area (magnitude $A$, direction normal to the loop). For the Earth, the equivalent $I$ is the geomagnetic current flowing in the molten outer core.

Field of a magnetic dipole at a distance $r$ from its centre:

ExpressionDirection
$\displaystyle \mathbf{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^{3}}\big[3(\mathbf{m}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})\hat{\mathbf r}-\mathbf{m}\big]$General vector form
$\displaystyle B_{\text{eq}}=\frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^{3}}$Equatorial plane ($\theta=90^{\circ}$)
$\displaystyle B_{\text{pole}}=\frac{2\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^{3}}$Polar axis ($\theta=0^{\circ}$)

SI units: $\mathbf{B}$ in tesla (T), $\mathbf{m}$ in ampere‑meter$^2$ (A·m$^2$), $r$ in metres (m), $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H·m$^{-1}$.

Derivation of $m$ for Earth: Using $B_{\text{pole}}$ measured at the surface ($r=R_E$), $$m=\frac{2\pi R_E^{3} B_{\text{pole}}}{\mu_0}.$$

Example – Find the Earth’s magnetic dipole moment given $B_{\text{pole}}=6.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$ and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}\,\text{m}$.

  • Insert values \in the formula: $$m=\frac{2\pi (6.37\times10^{6})^{3}(6.2\times10^{-5})}{4\pi\times10^{-7}}.$$
  • Compute $(6.37\times10^{6})^{3}=6.37^{3}\times10^{18}\approx2.58\times10^{2}\times10^{18}=2.58\times10^{20}$.
  • Numerator $=2\pi\times2.58\times10^{20}\times6.2\times10^{-5}\approx3.2\times10^{16}$.
  • Denominator $=4\pi\times10^{-7}=1.26\times10^{-6}$.
  • Thus $m\approx\frac{3.2\times10^{16}}{1.26\times10^{-6}}\approx2.5\times10^{22}\,\text{A·m}^2$ (more accurate calculation gives $\sim8\times10^{22}\,\text{A·m}^2$).

The result shows that the Earth’s magnetic dipole moment is of order $10^{22}$ A·m$^2$, confirming the dipole approximation’s validity for most practical problems in magnetism.
long_notes.Magnetic field of a solenoid and toroid:
Magnetic field of a solenoid

A solenoid is a long coil of $N$ turns uniformly wound over length $L$. The field inside a tightly wound, infinitely long solenoid is uniform and given by
$$B=\mu_0 n I$$
where $n=\frac{N}{L}$ (turns per metre) and $I$ is the current. The direction follows the \right‑hand rule. Outside the solenoid $B\approx0$. SI unit of $B$ is the tesla (T).

Magnetic field of a toroid

A toroid is a solenoid bent into a circular ring of mean radius $r$. Using Ampère’s circuital law for a circular path inside the core, the field is
$$B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$$
The field is confined within the core; outside it is practically zero. $N$ is total turns, $I$ the current, and $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{H m}^{-1}$.

Key symbols

SymbolMeaningSI unit
$B$Magnetic flux densityT
$\mu_0$Permeability of free spaceH·m$^{-1}$
$n$Turns per unit lengthm$^{-1}$
$I$CurrentA
$r$Mean radius of toroidm

Example

Find the magnetic field at the centre of a long solenoid having $N=500$ turns, length $L=0.20\,\text{m}$ and carrying a current $I=2\,\text{A}$.

  • Turns per metre $n=\frac{N}{L}=\frac{500}{0.20}=2500\,\text{m}^{-1}$.
  • Using $B=\mu_0 n I$,
    $$B=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2500\times2=6.28\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$$

Thus the solenoid produces a uniform field of $6.3\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$ inside.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Magnetic Field ($\\vec{B}$): Vector field representing the magnetic influence of moving charges or currents; direction given by the force on a north pole.
  • Magnetic Flux ($\\Phi$): $\\Phi = \\int \\vec{B}\cdot d\\vec{A}$ – total field passing through a surface.
  • Right Hand Thumb Rule: Thumb along current direction, curled fingers give direction of $\\vec{B}$ around a straight conductor.
  • Right Hand Grip Rule: Curl fingers along current in a coil; thumb points along the magnetic moment $\\vec{\mu}$ (field inside the coil).
  • Faraday’s Law of Electromagnetic Induction: $\\mathcal{E}= -N\\frac{d\\Phi}{dt}$ – induced emf equals negative rate of change of flux (Lenz’s law gives direction).
  • Lenz’s Law: The induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
  • Ampère’s Law (Integral Form): $\\oint \\vec{B}\cdot d\\vec{l}=\\mu_0 I_{enc}$ – relates magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through.
  • Biot–Savart Law: Gives $\\vec{B}$ due to an infinitesimal current element $d\\vec{l}$.
  • Magnetic Dipole Moment ($\\vec{\mu}$): $\\vec{\mu}= I A \\hat{n}$ – product of current and area vector of the loop.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick Summary

  • Use $F = q\\,\\vec{v}\\times\\vec{B}$ only when velocity is perpendicular to $\\vec{B}$; otherwise include $\sin\theta$.
  • For a solenoid, $B = \mu_0 n I$ (where $n$ = turns per unit length) – not to be confused with $B$ inside a toroid.
  • Direction of induced emf follows Lenz’s law, not the right‑hand rule alone.
  • When applying Ampère’s law, choose a path where $\\vec{B}$ is constant and parallel to $d\\vec{l}$; otherwise the integral must be evaluated piecewise.
  • Remember $\\Phi = B A \cos\theta$ – many students forget the $\cos\theta$ factor for inclined surfaces.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  1. Mixing up $\\vec{B}$ (magnetic field) with $\\vec{H}$ (magnetic field intensity). In free space $\\vec{B}=\mu_0\\vec{H}$.
  2. Ignoring the sign in Faraday’s law; the negative sign is crucial for Lenz’s law.
  3. Using $F = qvB$ for non‑perpendicular motion – always multiply by $\sin\theta$.
  4. Applying Biot–Savart law to infinite wires without limits – use Ampère’s law for such cases.
  5. For a coil, using $L = \mu_0 N^2 A / l$ without ensuring the coil is tightly wound and length $l$ >> radius.

numericals.question: A proton (charge $+e$, mass $1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$) enters a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.5\,\text{T}$ with speed $2\times10^{6}\,\text{m/s}$ perpendicular to the field. Find the radius of its circular trajectory.

A straight conductor of length $0.30\,\text{m}$ carries a current of $5\,\text{A}$ and is placed in a uniform magnetic field of $0.2\,\text{T}$ making an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the field direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force on the conductor.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=5\,\text{A}$, $L=0.30\,\text{m}$, $B=0.2\,\text{T}$, $\theta=30^{\circ}$
Formula: $F=BI L\sin\theta$
Solution: $F=0.2\times5\times0.30\times\sin30^{\circ}=0.2\times5\times0.30\times0.5=0.15\,\text{N}$
Direction: Use Fleming's left hand rule – force is perpendicular to both $I$ (along the conductor) and $B$, out of the page for the given orientation.
Answer: $F=0.15\,\text{N}$ (out of the page)

numericals.question: A rectangular current loop of dimensions $4\,\text{cm}\times6\,\text{cm}$ carries a current of $2\,\text{A}$. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of $0.1\,\text{T}$ such that the plane of the loop makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the field. Find the torque acting on the loop.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=2\,\text{A}$, $A=4\times6\,\text{cm}^{2}=24\,\text{cm}^{2}=2.4\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{2}$, $B=0.1\,\text{T}$, $\theta=45^{\circ}$
Formula: $\tau=BI A\sin\theta$
Solution: $\tau=0.1\times2\times2.4\times10^{-3}\times\sin45^{\circ}=0.2\times2.4\times10^{-3}\times\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=0.2\times2.4\times10^{-3}\times0.707=3.39\times10^{-4}\,\text{N·m}$
Answer: $\tau\approx3.4\times10^{-4}\,\text{N·m}$

numericals.question: A long straight wire carries a current of $3\,\text{A}$. Find the magnetic field at a point $P$ located $5\,\text{cm}$ from the wire.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=3\,\text{A}$, $r=5\,\text{cm}=0.05\,\text{m}$
Formula: $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2\pi r}$, where $\mu_{0}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T·m/A}$
Solution: $B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3}{2\pi\times0.05}=\frac{12\pi\times10^{-7}}{0.1\pi}=1.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$
Answer: $B=1.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$ (directed tangentially according to the right‑hand rule)

long_notes.Magnetic field: definition, lines of for:
Definition: The magnetic field $ \vec B$ at a point is defined as the force per unit positive test charge moving with velocity $ \vec v$ perpendicular to the field, i.e., $ \vec B = rac{ \vec F}{q\,v\,\sin heta}$. Its SI unit is the tesla (T), where $1\, ext{T}= rac{ ext{N}}{ ext{A}\, ext{m}}$.

Lines of magnetic force

  • They are continuous loops; they never begin or end.
  • Direction of a line at any point is tangent to the direction of $ \vec B$.
  • Density of lines (lines per unit area) is proportional to the magnitude of $ \vec B$.
  • Lines never intersect each other.

Key formula for a long straight conductor

From the Biot–Savart law, the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance $r$ from a straight wire carrying current $I$ is

$$ \vec B = rac{ \mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$

where $ \mu_0 = 4\pi imes10^{-7}\, ext{T·m/A}$.

SI Units

QuantitySymbolUnit
Magnetic field$ \vec B$tesla (T)
Current$I$ampere (A)
Permeability of free space$ \mu_0$T·m/A

Solved example

Problem: A long straight wire carries $I=10\, ext{A}$. Find the magnetic field $B$ at a point $5\, ext{cm}$ from the wire.

Solution: Convert $r=5\, ext{cm}=0.05\, ext{m}$. Using $B= rac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$,

$$ \vec B = rac{(4\pi imes10^{-7}) imes10}{2\pi imes0.05}= rac{4\pi imes10^{-6}}{0.1\pi}=4 imes10^{-5}\, ext{T}$$

Thus $B=4 imes10^{-5}\, ext{T}$ directed azimuthally according to the right‑hand rule.
long_notes.Motion of charged particles in a magneti:
Magnetic force on a moving charge: When a charge $q$ moves with velocity $\\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\\vec{B}$, it experiences a force $\\vec{F}=q\\,\\vec{v}\\times\\vec{B}$ (SI unit N). The magnitude is $F=|q|vB\\sin\\theta$, where $\\theta$ is the angle between $\\vec{v}$ and $\\vec{B}$.

Uniform field, $90^\\circ$ leads to uniform circular motion. Equating magnetic force to centripetal force $\\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ gives

$r=\\frac{mv}{|q|B}$, $T=\\frac{2\\pi m}{|q|B}$, $f=\\frac{|q|B}{2\\pi m}$.

Key formulas:

QuantityFormulaSI unit
Radius $r$$r=\\frac{mv}{|q|B}$m
Period $T$$T=\\frac{2\\pi m}{|q|B}$s
Frequency $f$$f=\\frac{|q|B}{2\\pi m}$Hz

Example:

A proton ($m=1.67\\times10^{-27}\\,\\text{kg}$, $q=+e=1.60\\times10^{-19}\\,\\text{C}$) enters a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\\,\\text{T}$ perpendicular to its velocity $v=2\\times10^{6}\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the radius of its path and the cyclotron frequency.

  • Radius $r=\\frac{mv}{qB}=\\frac{(1.67\\times10^{-27})(2\\times10^{6})}{(1.60\\times10^{-19})(0.5)}\\approx4.2\\times10^{-2}\\,\\text{m}$.
  • Frequency $f=\\frac{qB}{2\\pi m}=\\frac{(1.60\\times10^{-19})(0.5)}{2\\pi(1.67\\times10^{-27})}\\approx7.6\\times10^{6}\\,\\text{Hz}$.

Thus the proton moves in a circular orbit of radius $\\approx4.2\\,\\text{cm}$ with a cyclotron frequency of $\\approx7.6\\,\\text{MHz}$.
long_notes.Force on a current‑carrying conductor an:
Force on a current‑carrying conductor

When a conductor of length $\ell$ carrying current $I$ is placed in a magnetic field $B$, the magnetic force on it is given by

$$F = I\,\ell\,B\,\sin\theta$$

Derivation: The drift velocity of charge carriers is $v_d$. For $n$ carriers per unit volume, charge $q$, the current $I = n q A v_d$. The Lorentz force on each carrier is $q\,v_d\,B\,\sin\theta$. Multiplying by the total number of carriers \in the segment $n A \ell$ gives $F = I \ell B \sin\theta$.

SI unit: newton (N).

Hall effect

When a magnetic field $B$ is applied perpendicular \to the direction of current $I$ \in a thin slab of thickness $t$, charge carriers accumulate on one side, creating a transverse Hall voltage $V_H$:

$$V_H = \frac{I B}{n e t} = R_H \frac{I B}{t}$$

Hall coefficient $R_H = \frac{1}{n e}$ (unit $m^3 C^{-1}$). $V_H$ is measured \in volts (V).

SymbolFormulaUnit
$F$$I\,\ell\,B\,\sin\theta$$N$
$V_H$$\frac{I B}{n e t}$$V$
$R_H$$\frac{1}{n e}$$m^3 C^{-1}$

Example

Find the magnetic force on a 5 m long wire carrying $3\,\text{A}$ placed perpendicular ($\theta=90^\circ$) \to a uniform magnetic field of $0.2\,\text{T}$.

Solution: $F = I\,\ell\,B = 3 \times 5 \times 0.2 = 3\,\text{N}$.
long_notes.Torque on a current loop and magnetic di:
Torque on a current loop – When a planar loop carrying current $I$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, each side experiences a magnetic force $d\mathbf{F}=I\,d\mathbf{l}\times\mathbf{B}$. The resultant couple about the centre is called the torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.

Magnetic dipole moment – For any closed loop the vector quantity

SymbolExpressionSI unit
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$$I\mathbf{A}$$\text{A·m}^2$

where $\mathbf{A}=A\hat{n}$ is the area vector (magnitude $A$ and direction $\hat{n}$ normal to the plane).

Key formula

  • $\boldsymbol{\tau}= \boldsymbol{\mu}\times\mathbf{B}$
  • Magnitude: $\tau = IAB\sin\theta$

SI unit of torque: newton‑metre (N·m). $I$ in ampere (A), $A$ in square metre (m$^2$), $B$ in tesla (T), $\theta$ the angle between $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Derivation (brief)

Consider a rectangular loop of sides $l$ and $w$. Forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite, producing a couple $F l = I B w \; l$. Adding the contribution from the other pair gives $\tau = I B (l w)\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$, which is independent of the shape, leading to the vector form $\boldsymbol{\tau}= \boldsymbol{\mu}\times\mathbf{B}$.

Example

A rectangular loop $0.10\ \text{m}\times0.20\ \text{m}$ carries $I=5\ \text{A}$. It is placed in a uniform field $B=0.30\ \text{T}$ making $\theta=30^\circ$ with the normal. Area $A=0.10\times0.20=0.020\ \text{m}^2$. Magnetic moment $\mu = I A =5\times0.020=0.10\ \text{A·m}^2$. Torque $\tau = \mu B\sin\theta =0.10\times0.30\times\sin30^\circ =0.015\ \text{N·m}$.
long_notes.Earth’s magnetic field and magnetic decl:
Earth’s Magnetic Field

  • Definition: The magnetic field produced by the Earth behaves like a giant bar‑magnet whose magnetic dipole moment $M$ is aligned approximately along the geographic axis.
  • SI unit: $B$ – tesla (T); $M$ – ampere‑meter$^2$ (A·m$^2$).
  • Dipole formula (at surface, $r=R_E$): $$B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2M}{R_E^3}$$ where $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{H·m}^{-1}$.
  • Components: Horizontal $B_H = B\cos I$, vertical $B_V = B\sin I$, where $I$ is magnetic inclination.

Magnetic Declination ($D$)

  • Angle between geographic north (true north) and magnetic north (direction of $B_H$).
  • Positive eastward, negative westward. Measured \in degrees ($^\circ$).
SymbolMeaningUnit
$B$Resultant magnetic fieldT
$B_H$Horizontal componentT
$B_V$Vertical componentT
$I$Magnetic inclination°
$D$Magnetic declination°

Solved Example

Given $B = 5.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$ and $I = 60^\circ$, find $B_H$ and $B_V$.

Solution:

  • $B_H = B\cos I = 5.0\times10^{-5}\cos60^\circ = 5.0\times10^{-5}\times0.5 = 2.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$
  • $B_V = B\sin I = 5.0\times10^{-5}\sin60^\circ = 5.0\times10^{-5}\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 4.33\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$

Thus $B_H = 2.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$ and $B_V = 4.33\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$.
long_notes.Magnetic materials: diamagnetism, parama:
Magnetic Materials

  • Diamagnetism: All atoms develop an induced magnetic moment opposite to the applied field. $\chi < 0$ (dimensionless). $\vec{M}= \chi \vec{H}$ with $\chi$ small ($\sim -10^{-5}$). No permanent magnetic moment.
  • Paramagnetism: Materials possess permanent atomic moments that align partially with $\vec{H}$. $\chi > 0$ and follows Curie’s law $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$, where $C$ is Curie constant. Magnetization $M = \chi H = \dfrac{C}{T} H$.
  • Ferromagnetism: Strong exchange interaction aligns moments parallel even without $\vec{H}$. Below Curie temperature $T_C$, spontaneous magnetization $M_s$ appears. Above $T_C$, susceptibility obeys Curie‑Weiss law $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T-\theta}$ with $\theta \approx T_C$. Weiss molecular field $H_{eff}=H+\lambda M$.

Key Relations

QuantitySymbolExpressionSI Unit
Magnetization$M$$M=\chi H$A·m$^{-1}$
Magnetic susceptibility$\chi$dimensionless–
Curie law (paramagnets)$\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$–
Curie‑Weiss law (ferromagnets)$\chi = \dfrac{C}{T-\theta}$–
Weiss field constant$\lambda$$H_{eff}=H+\lambda M$A·m$^{-1}$

Solved Example

Given $C = 1.5\ \text{K·emu·mol}^{-1}$, $T = 300\ \text{K}$ and $H = 10^{4}\ \text{A·m}^{-1}$, find $M$.

  1. Compute susceptibility: $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}= \dfrac{1.5}{300}=5.0\times10^{-3}$.
  2. Magnetization: $M = \chi H = 5.0\times10^{-3}\times10^{4}=50\ \text{A·m}^{-1}$.

Thus the paramagnetic sample acquires $M = 50\ \text{A·m}^{-1}$ under the given field.
long_notes.Magnetic hysteresis, domains and Curie t:
Magnetic Hysteresis, Domains and Curie Temperature

When a ferromagnetic material is subjected to a cyclic magnetizing field $H$, the magnetic induction $B$ does not retrace the same path; the $B$–$H$ curve forms a hysteresis loop. The loop is characterised by:

  • Retentivity (or remanent induction) $B_{r}$: $B$ remaining when $H$ is reduced to zero (unit: $\text{T}$).
  • Coercivity $H_{c}$: magnitude of reverse field required to bring $B$ to zero (unit: $\text{A/m}$).
  • Loop area: proportional to energy loss per unit volume per cycle, $W = \text{area}$ (unit: $\text{J/m}^3$).

Fundamental relations:

SymbolDefinitionFormulaSI Unit
$B$Magnetic induction$B = \mu_{0}(H+M)$T
$H$Magnetizing field–A/m
$M$Magnetisation$M = \chi H$A/m
$\mu$Permeability$\mu = \frac{B}{H}$–
$\chi$Magnetic susceptibility$\chi = \frac{M}{H}$–

Ferromagnetic materials consist of magnetic domains – regions where atomic moments are aligned. In the unmagnetised state, domains are randomly oriented, giving net $M=0$. An external $H$ grows favourably aligned domains, producing macroscopic magnetisation.

Curie Temperature $T_{C}$ is the temperature at which spontaneous magnetisation vanishes and the material becomes paramagnetic. Above $T_{C}$ the susceptibility follows the Curie‑Weiss law:

$$\chi = \frac{C}{T - T_{C}}$$

where $C$ is the Curie constant (unit: K). At $T=T_{C}$, $\chi$ diverges.

Example: A ferromagnet shows a rectangular hysteresis loop with $B_{r}=0.8\,\text{T}$ and $H_{c}=200\,\text{A/m}$. Approximate the energy loss per unit volume per cycle.

For a rectangular loop, $W \approx 4 B_{r} H_{c}$. Hence

$$W = 4 \times 0.8 \times 200 = 640\,\text{J/m}^3$$

The material loses $640\,\text{J}$ of energy per cubic metre each magnetisation cycle.
long_notes.Electromagnetic induction: Faraday’s law:
Electromagnetic Induction – When a magnetic flux through a circuit changes with time, an emf is induced in the circuit.

Faraday’s law (integral form):

$$\mathcal{E}= -\,\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$

For a coil of $N$ turns, $$\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$ where $\Phi = B A\cos\theta$.

  • SI unit of emf: $V$ (volt).
  • SI unit of magnetic flux: $Wb$ (weber) = $T\;m^{2}$.

Lenz’s law – The direction of the induced emf is such that the induced current opposes the change producing it.

SymbolMeaningSI Unit
$\mathcal{E}$Induced emf$V$
$\Phi$Magnetic flux$Wb$
$B$Magnetic flux density$T$
$A$Area of coil$m^{2}$
$N$Number of turns–

Key derivation (emf for a rotating coil)

For a coil rotating with angular speed $\omega$ \in a uniform $B$, $\Phi = B A\cos\omega t$. Hence $$\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d}{dt}(B A\cos\omega t)= N B A\omega\sin\omega t$$ and the maximum emf $$\mathcal{E}_{\max}= N B A\omega$$.

Example

A rectangular coil of $N=50$ turns, area $A=0.02\;m^{2}$ rotates at $\omega =60\;rad\,s^{-1}$ \in a magnetic field $B=0.5\;T$. Find the peak emf.

Solution:

$$\mathcal{E}_{\max}= N B A\omega = 50\times0.5\times0.02\times60 = 30\;V$$

Thus the coil produces a sinusoidal emf of amplitude $30\;V$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Magnetic Field ($\mathbf{B}$): Vector field representing the magnetic influence of electric currents and magnetic materials.
  • Magnetic Intensity ($\mathbf{H}$): Field produced by free currents; related to $\mathbf{B}$ by $\mathbf{B}=\mu_0(\mathbf{H}+\mathbf{M})$.
  • Magnetization ($\mathbf{M}$): Magnetic moment per unit volume of a material.
  • Magnetic Susceptibility ($\chi_m$): Dimensionless constant $\chi_m=\frac{\mathbf{M}}{\mathbf{H}}$ indicating how a material responds to $\mathbf{H}$.
  • Permeability ($\mu$): Measure of the ability of a material to support the formation of a magnetic field, $\mu=\mu_0\mu_r$.
  • Biot‑Savart Law: Gives $\mathbf{B}$ due to a small current element; fundamental for calculating magnetic fields of arbitrary shapes.
  • Ampère’s Law: Relates the integrated magnetic field around a closed loop to the net current passing through the loop.
  • Right Hand Rule: Thumb along current direction, fingers curl to show direction of $\mathbf{B}$.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Summary: Magnetism in matter links $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{H}$, and $\mathbf{M}$ through $\mathbf{B}=\mu_0(\mathbf{H}+\mathbf{M})$. For linear, isotropic media $\mathbf{M}=\chi_m\mathbf{H}$, giving $\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\mu_r\mathbf{H}$. Use Biot‑Savart for elemental contributions and Ampère’s law for symmetry‑driven problems. Remember torque $\tau=\mu B\sin\theta$ and force $\mathbf{F}=I\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{B}$.

Common Mistakes:

  • Confusing $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{H}$; $\mathbf{B}$ includes material response, $\mathbf{H}$ does not.
  • Omitting $\mu_0$ in formulas for $\mathbf{B}$ in vacuum.
  • Using $\chi_m$ instead of $\mu_r$ without adding 1 (i.e., $\mu_r=1+\chi_m$).
  • Sign error in cross‑product for force/torque; direction follows right‑hand rule.
  • Applying Ampère’s law to non‑closed paths or ignoring enclosed current.

numericals.question: A long straight wire carries a current of $5\,\text{A}$. Find the magnetic field at a point $2\,\text{cm}$ from the wire.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=5\,\text{A}$, $r=2\,\text{cm}=0.02\,\text{m}$.

Formula: $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

Calculation: $B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times5}{2\pi\times0.02}=\frac{2\times10^{-6}\times5}{0.04}=\frac{1\times10^{-5}}{0.04}=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

Answer: $B=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

numericals.question: A rectangular loop of dimensions $10\,\text{cm}\times5\,\text{cm}$ carries a current of $3\,\text{A}$ and lies in a uniform magnetic field of $0.2\,\text{T}$, with the plane of the loop parallel to the field. Find the magnitude of the force on each side of the loop.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=3\,\text{A}$, $B=0.2\,\text{T}$, length of side parallel to $B$ $=10\,\text{cm}=0.10\,\text{m}$, length of side perpendicular to $B$ $=5\,\text{cm}=0.05\,\text{m}$.

Formula: $F=IBL\sin\theta$.

Calculation: For sides parallel to $B$, $\theta=0^\circ$, $F=IBL\sin0=0$.
For sides perpendicular to $B$, $\theta=90^\circ$, $F=IBL=3\times0.2\times0.05=0.03\,\text{N}$.

Answer: Force on each side parallel to $B$ is $0\,\text{N}$; force on each side perpendicular to $B$ is $0.03\,\text{N}$ (directed opposite on the two sides).

numericals.question: A square loop of side $8\,\text{cm}$ carries a current of $2\,\text{A}$ and is placed in a uniform magnetic field of $0.5\,\text{T}$, the plane of the loop making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the field direction. Find the torque acting on the loop.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $I=2\,\text{A}$, $a=8\,\text{cm}=0.08\,\text{m}$, $B=0.5\,\text{T}$, $\theta=30^\circ$.

Formula: $\tau = B I A \sin\theta$, where $A=a^2$.

Calculation: $A=(0.08)^2=6.4\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2$.
$\tau =0.5\times2\times6.4\times10^{-3}\times\sin30^\circ =1\times6.4\times10^{-3}\times0.5=3.2\times10^{-3}\,\text{N·m}$.

Answer: $\tau =3.2\times10^{-3}\,\text{N·m}$.

numericals.question: Find the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius $5\,\text{cm}$ carrying a current of $4\,\text{A}$. The coil has $N=10$ turns.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $R=5\,\text{cm}=0.05\,\text{m}$, $I=4\,\text{A}$, $N=10$.

Formula: $B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$.

Calculation: $B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10\times4}{2\times0.05}=\frac{1.6\pi\times10^{-5}}{0.1}=1.6\pi\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}\approx5.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

Answer: $B\approx5.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$ at the centre.

numericals.question: Two long parallel conductors are $15\,\text{cm}$ apart and carry currents $I_1=6\,\text{A}$ and $I_2=8\,\text{A}$ in the same direction. Find the force per unit length between them.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $d=15\,\text{cm}=0.15\,\text{m}$, $I_1=6\,\text{A}$, $I_2=8\,\text{A}$.

Formula: $\frac{F}{L}=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.

Calculation: $\frac{F}{L}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times6\times8}{2\pi\times0.15}=\frac{192\pi\times10^{-7}}{0.3\pi}=\frac{192\times10^{-7}}{0.3}=6.4\times10^{-4}\,\text{N/m}$.

Answer: $\frac{F}{L}=6.4\times10^{-4}\,\text{N/m}$ (attractive).

pyq.question: State the Biot–Savart law for a small element of a current‑carrying conductor.
pyq.answer_html: For a current element $I\,d\ell$ at a point P, the magnetic field $d\mathbf{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\ell\times\hat{r}}{r^{2}}$, where $\hat{r}$ is the unit vector from the element to P and $r$ is the distance.

pyq.question: Define the magnetic moment $\mathbf{\mu}$ of a planar current loop.
pyq.answer_html: The magnetic moment $\mathbf{\mu}$ is given by $\mathbf{\mu}=I\,\mathbf{A}$, where $I$ is the current and $\mathbf{A}$ is the vector area (magnitude = area of loop, direction normal to the plane following the right‑hand rule).

pyq.question: A rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ carries a current $I$. Find its magnetic dipole moment.
pyq.answer_html: The area of the loop $A=ab$. Using $\mu=I A$, the magnetic dipole moment $\mu=I\,ab$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop (right‑hand rule).

pyq.question: Explain why the magnetic field inside a long solenoid is uniform and give its expression.
pyq.answer_html: Inside a long solenoid the field lines are parallel and densely packed, making $\mathbf{B}$ nearly uniform. Using Ampère's law for a rectangular Amperian loop of length $l$ inside the solenoid, $\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=\mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}$, we obtain $B=\mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

pyq.question: A circular coil of radius $R=10\,\text{cm}$ has $N=200$ turns and carries a current $I=2\,\text{A}$. Derive the expression for the magnetic field at the centre of the coil and calculate its magnitude.
pyq.answer_html:
For a single turn, $B_{\text{single}}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$. For $N$ turns, $B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$. Substituting $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T·m/A}$, $N=200$, $I=2\,\text{A}$ and $R=0.10\,\text{m}$:
$B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times200\times2}{2\times0.10}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times400}{0.20}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000}{1}=8\pi\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}\approx2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$.

pyq.question: Explain the hysteresis loop of a ferromagnetic material and define coercivity, retentivity and saturation magnetization.
pyq.answer_html:
The hysteresis loop is the $B$–$H$ curve obtained when a ferromagnetic specimen is cycled through a complete magnetisation–demagnetisation cycle. Key points:
\textbf{Saturation magnetization ($M_s$)}: the maximum magnetisation when all domains are aligned; corresponds to the flat top of the loop.
\textbf{Retentivity (or remanence, $B_r$)}: the residual magnetic flux density left in the material when the external field $H$ is reduced to zero; it is the $B$ value at $H=0$ on the descending branch.
\textbf{Coercivity ($H_c$)}: the magnitude of reverse field required to reduce the flux density to zero; it is the $H$ value at $B=0$ on the descending branch.
The area of the loop represents energy loss per cycle.

mcq.q: The magnetic field at a distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is given by
mcq.explain: Using Ampère's circuital law for a straight conductor, $\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=\mu_0 I_{enc}$ gives $B(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I \Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

mcq.q: A rectangular loop of area $A$ carries current $I$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The magnitude of the torque on the loop is
mcq.explain: Torque $\tau = \mathbf{\mu}\times \mathbf{B}$ with magnetic dipole moment $\mu = IA$ and $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$, so $\tau = IAB$.

mcq.q: The magnetic dipole moment of a current loop is
mcq.explain: By definition, $\mu = I\times \text{area}$ vector normal to the plane of the loop.

mcq.q: A charge $q$ moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$. The magnetic force on the charge is
mcq.explain: Lorentz force $\mathbf{F}=q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$; for $\mathbf{v}\perp\mathbf{B}$, $F = qvB$.

mcq.q: In the Hall effect experiment, the Hall voltage is directly proportional to
mcq.explain: Hall voltage $V_H = \frac{IB}{ned}$; it varies linearly with $B$ (and also with $I$, but the primary proportionality asked is with $B$).

mcq.q: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid (length $\gg$ radius) carrying current $I$ is
mcq.explain: For an ideal solenoid, $B=\mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is turns per unit length.

mcq.q: A material with magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m = -1.0\times10^{-5}$ is
mcq.explain: Negative susceptibility indicates diamagnetism.

mcq.q: Paramagnetic substances differ from diamagnetic substances because
mcq.explain: Paramagnets have small positive susceptibility; diamagnets have small negative susceptibility.

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): The Earth’s magnetic field is directed from the geographic south to the geographic north.
Reason (R): The magnetic north pole of the Earth is actually a magnetic south pole.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: The field lines emerge from the magnetic south pole (geographic north) and enter the magnetic north pole (geographic south); thus the field direction is from geographic south to north, and the magnetic north pole is indeed a magnetic south pole, so R explains A.

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): A thin copper sheet can shield a region from external magnetic fields.
Reason (R): Copper is a good conductor and supports induced eddy currents that oppose the change in magnetic flux.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Conducting sheets produce eddy currents (Lenz’s law) that oppose time‑varying magnetic fields, providing magnetic shielding; thus both statements are true and R explains A.

long_notes.Induced EMF and Faraday's law:
Induced EMF (Electromotive Force) – The voltage generated in a closed circuit when the magnetic flux through the circuit changes with time.

Faraday’s Law

  • For a single turn: $\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$
  • For $N$ turns: $\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$

where $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ is the magnetic flux ($B$ – magnetic field in tesla, $A$ – area in $m^2$, $\theta$ – angle between $B$ and normal to the loop).

Lenz’s Law – The direction of the induced emf is such that the induced current creates a magnetic field opposing the change in original flux.

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Induced emf$\mathcal{E}$$-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$V
Magnetic flux$\Phi$$BA\cos\theta$Wb
Motional emf$Blv$V

Derivation (motional emf): A straight conductor of length $l$ moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. The magnetic force on charge $q$ is $F = qvB$. Since $F = q\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{E}=vBl$.

Example:

A rectangular loop of width $0.1\,$m and height $0.2\,$m is pulled out of a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\,$T at a constant speed $v=0.3\,$m/s. Find the induced emf while the loop is leaving the field.

Only the side of length $0.2\,$m cuts the flux. Using $\mathcal{E}=Blv$, $\mathcal{E}=0.5\times0.2\times0.3=0.03\,$V. The polarity is such that the induced current opposes the decrease of flux (Lenz’s law).
long_notes.Lenz's law and its applications:
Definition (Lenz’s Law): The induced emf in a closed circuit always opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.

Mathematical Form:

  • Induced emf $\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}$
  • Direction given by right‑hand rule for the induced current.

Key Derivation:

StepExpression
Magnetic flux$\\Phi = \\int \\mathbf{B}\\cdot d\\mathbf{A}$
Faraday’s law$\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}$
Using $\\mathcal{E}= -N\\dfrac{d\\phi}{dt}$ for $N$ turns$\\mathcal{E}= -N\\dfrac{d}{dt}(BA\\cos\\theta)$

SI Units: emf – volt (V), magnetic flux – weber (Wb), magnetic field – tesla (T), area – $\\text{m}^2$.

Applications:

  • Eddy current brakes
  • Induction cookers
  • Metal detectors
  • Generators and transformers

Example (Solved): A rectangular loop $0.10\\,\\text{m}\\times0.20\\,\\text{m}$ moves with speed $v=2\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$ into a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\\,\\text{T}$ perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Find the magnitude of the induced emf when the loop is partially inside the field.

Solution: Flux $\\Phi = B\\,l\\,x$, where $x$ is the length inside the field. $\\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v$, so $\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}= -B\\,l\\,\\dfrac{dx}{dt}= -B\\,l\\,v$. Substituting $B=0.5\\,\\text{T}$, $l=0.20\\,\\text{m}$, $v=2\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$ gives $\\mathcal{E}= -(0.5)(0.20)(2)= -0.20\\,\\text{V}$. Magnitude $=0.20\\,\\text{V}$.
long_notes.Self induction and mutual induction:
Self Induction – When a time‑varying current $i(t)$ flows through a coil, the changing magnetic flux linked with the coil itself induces an emf $\\mathcal{E}$ that opposes the change (Lenz’s law).

  • Flux linkage $\\lambda = N\\Phi$.
  • Induced emf $\\mathcal{E} = -\\dfrac{d\\lambda}{dt}= -L\\dfrac{di}{dt}$.
  • Self‑inductance $L = \\dfrac{N\\Phi}{i}$, SI unit henry (H) = $\\dfrac{Wb}{A}$.

Mutual Induction – A varying current in one coil (primary) produces a changing flux that links a second coil (secondary), inducing an emf in the latter.

  • Mutual inductance $M = \\dfrac{N_2\\Phi_{12}}{i_1}=\\dfrac{N_1\\Phi_{21}}{i_2}$.
  • Induced emf in secondary $\\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\\dfrac{di_1}{dt}$.
  • SI unit also henry.

Key Relations

QuantityExpression
Self‑inductance $L$$L = \\dfrac{\\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$ (solenoid)
Mutual inductance $M$$M = k\\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, $0\\le k\\le1$
Energy stored$U = \\dfrac{1}{2}Li^2 = \\dfrac{1}{2}Mi_1i_2$

Example

A solenoid has $N=500$ turns, length $l=0.20\\,\\text{m}$, cross‑section $A=2\\times10^{-4}\\,\\text{m}^2$. The current changes at $\\dfrac{di}{dt}=3\\,\\text{A s}^{-1}$. Find the induced emf.

Solution:

  1. Compute $L = \\dfrac{\\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}=\\dfrac{4\\pi\\times10^{-7}\\times 500^2\\times2\\times10^{-4}}{0.20}=\\,\\text{... H}$ → $L\\approx 1.57\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{H}$.
  2. Induced emf $|\\mathcal{E}| = L\\dfrac{di}{dt}=1.57\\times10^{-3}\\times3\\approx4.7\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{V}$.

Thus $\\mathcal{E}\\approx4.7\\,\\text{mV}$, opposing the increase of current.
long_notes.Eddy currents and their effects:
Definition: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in a bulk conductor when it is subjected to a time‑varying magnetic flux. They flow in closed loops perpendicular to the magnetic field and oppose the change in flux (Lenz's law).

Cause & Effect:

  • Relative motion between a conductor and magnetic field or a varying field induces emf $e=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$.
  • Resulting currents produce magnetic fields that oppose motion – used in magnetic braking, induction heating, and levitation.
  • Energy dissipated as heat: $P=I^{2}R$.

Key Formulas

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Induced emf$e$$e=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$volt (V)
Current density (thin plate)$J$$J=\sigma B v$ampere per square metre (A/m$^2$)
Power loss (laminated plate)$P$$P=\frac{B^{2} t^{2} v^{2}}{6\rho}\,A$watt (W)

Mitigation: Use laminated cores, high‑resistivity alloys, or slotted conductors to break the current paths.

Example

A copper plate of thickness $t=2\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}$, width $w=0.10\,\text{m}$ and length $l=0.20\,\text{m}$ moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\,\text{T}$ with speed $v=5\,\text{m/s}$. Copper resistivity $\rho=1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. Find the eddy‑current power loss.

Solution:

  1. Area $A = w\times l = 0.10\times0.20 = 0.020\,\text{m}^2$.
  2. Use $P=\frac{B^{2} t^{2} v^{2}}{6\rho}\,A$.
  3. Substitute: $P = \frac{(0.5)^{2}(2\times10^{-3})^{2}(5)^{2}}{6\times1.68\times10^{-8}}\times0.020$.
  4. Calculate numerator: $(0.5)^{2}=0.25$, $(2\times10^{-3})^{2}=4\times10^{-6}$, $(5)^{2}=25$ → $0.25\times4\times10^{-6}\times25 = 2.5\times10^{-5}$.
  5. Denominator: $6\times1.68\times10^{-8}=1.008\times10^{-7}$.
  6. $P = \frac{2.5\times10^{-5}}{1.008\times10^{-7}}\times0.020 \approx 248\,\text{W}$.

Thus the moving plate dissipates approximately $2.5\times10^{2}\,\text{W}$ as heat due to eddy currents.
long_notes.Alternating current (AC) generator and d:
AC Generator (Alternator) – A device that converts mechanical rotation into alternating emf by the principle of electromagnetic induction. When a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates in a uniform magnetic field $B$, the magnetic flux through the coil is $\Phi = N B A \cos \theta$, where $\theta = \omega t$.

Differentiating, the induced emf is
$$\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= N B A \omega \sin \omega t$$

  • Peak emf $E_{0}=N B A \omega$ (unit: V)
  • RMS emf $E_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
  • Angular speed $\omega =2\pi f$ (rad/s), $f$ \in Hz

Dynamos (DC Generators) – An AC generator equipped with a split‑ring commutator that reverses the connection of the coil every half‑turn, delivering unidirectional (DC) output. The generated emf is

$$E = \frac{P \Phi Z N}{60 A}$$

  • $P$ – number of poles
  • $\Phi$ – flux per pole (Wb)
  • $Z$ – total conductors
  • $N$ – speed \in r.p.m.
  • $A$ – number of parallel paths

Key Units

QuantitySI Unit
Magnetic field $B$tesla (T)
Area $A$square metre (m$^2$)
Angular speed $\omega$radian per second (rad/s)
Emf $\mathcal{E}$volt (V)

Solved Example

Find the peak emf of a coil having $N=200$ turns, area $A=0.01\,\text{m}^2$, placed \in a magnetic field $B=0.5\,\text{T}$ and rotating at $50$ revolutions per second.

Angular speed $\omega =2\pi\times 50 =100\pi\,\text{rad/s}$.
Peak emf $E_{0}=N B A \omega =200\times0.5\times0.01\times100\pi =100\pi\,\text{V}\approx 314\,\text{V}$.

Thus the generator produces a sinusoidal emf of amplitude $\approx 314\,$V and rms value $\approx 222\,$V.
long_notes.Induction in solenoids, toroids and coil:
Induction in Solenoids, Toroids and Coils

When the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf $e$ is induced (Faraday’s law): $e=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$, where $N$ is the number of turns and $\Phi$ is the flux through one turn. The negative sign denotes Lenz’s law.

Key formulas

QuantityExpressionSI Unit
Flux through a solenoid$\Phi=BA=\mu_0 n I A$weber (Wb)
Induced emf (solenoid)$e=-\mu_0 n A\frac{dI}{dt}$volt (V)
Self‑inductance (solenoid)$L=\mu_0 n^2 A l$henry (H)
Magnetic field (toroid)$B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$tesla (T)
Flux per turn (toroid)$\Phi=\frac{\mu_0 N I A}{2\pi r}$Wb
Induced emf (toroid)$e=-\frac{\mu_0 N A}{2\pi r}\frac{dI}{dt}$V
Self‑inductance (toroid)$L=\frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{2\pi r}$H

SI Units

  • Inductance – henry (H) = V·s·A⁻¹
  • Magnetic flux – weber (Wb) = V·s

Example

A solenoid of length $l=0.5\,\text{m}$, $N=200$ turns and cross‑sectional area $A=2\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2$ carries a current that rises uniformly from $0$ to $3\,\text{A}$ in $0.02\,\text{s}$. Find the induced emf.

Solution:

  • Turns per unit length $n=\frac{N}{l}=\frac{200}{0.5}=400\,\text{turn/m}$.
  • Self‑inductance $L=\mu_0 n^2 A l=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times400^2\times2\times10^{-4}\times0.5\approx2.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{H}$.
  • Rate of change of current $\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{3-0}{0.02}=150\,\text{A/s}$.
  • Induced emf $e = L\frac{dI}{dt}=2.0\times10^{-5}\times150\approx3.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{V}$ (≈3 mV).

This result follows directly from $e = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$, confirming Lenz’s law (the emf opposes the increase of current).
long_notes.Energy stored in magnetic fields and ind:
Energy stored in magnetic field

When a current $I$ flows through an inductor of inductance $L$, a magnetic field is set up. The work done in establishing this field is stored as magnetic potential energy $U$.

  • Definition: $U$ is the energy required to build the magnetic field from zero to its final value.
  • Derivation: $dU = V_L\,dQ = L I\,dI$ (since $V_L = L\,dI/dt$ and $dQ = I\,dt$). Integrating, $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$.
  • SI unit: joule (J). $L$ in henry (H), $I$ in ampere (A).
  • Energy density in a uniform magnetic field: $u = \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_0}$ (J/m$^{3}$).

Energy in terms of flux linkage

For a coil with $N$ turns, flux linkage $\lambda = N\Phi$. Energy can also be written as $U = \frac{1}{2\lambda}\,\lambda^{2}= \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$ where $L = \lambda/I$.

QuantitySymbolFormulaUnit
Inductance$L$$L = \frac{N\Phi}{I}$henry (H)
Magnetic energy$U$$U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$joule (J)

Example

Find the energy stored in a $5\,$H inductor carrying $2\,$A.

Solution: $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\times5\times(2)^{2}= \frac{1}{2}\times5\times4 = 10\,$J.
long_notes.Practical applications of electromagneti:
Definition: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an emf ($e$) in a closed circuit when the magnetic flux linking the circuit changes with time.

Fundamental formula

QuantityExpressionSI unit
Induced emf$e = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$V

Practical applications

  • AC generator (alternator): Rotating coil in uniform $B$ gives $E_{max}=2\pi f N B A$. $f$ in Hz, $A$ in m$^2$.
  • Transformer: $\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p}$, ideal $P_{\in}=P_{out}$. Used for voltage step‑up/down.
  • Induction motor: Rotating magnetic field induces emf in rotor; torque $\tau = \frac{P}{\omega}$.
  • Eddy‑current brake: Relative motion of a conductor in $B$ produces opposing emf; braking force $F \propto B^2 v$.
  • Induction heating: Eddy currents $I$ in a metal produce heat $P = I^2 R \propto B^2 f^2 l^2$.

Solved example

A single‑layer coil of $N=200$ turns, area $A=0.01\,\text{m}^2$, rotates at $f=50\,\text{Hz}$ in a uniform magnetic field $B=0.2\,\text{T}$. Find the peak emf.

Solution:

  1. Angular speed $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi\times50 = 100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
  2. Peak emf $E_{max}= N B A \omega = 200\times0.2\times0.01\times100\pi = 4\pi\,\text{V}\approx 12.6\,\text{V}$.

Thus the generator would produce a sinusoidal emf of amplitude $\approx12.6\,$V.
