long_notes.Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors:
Intrinsic Semiconductor – a pure semiconductor crystal with no intentional impurity. At thermal equilibrium the electron ($n$) and hole ($p$) concentrations are equal:

  • $n = p = n_i$
  • Intrinsic carrier concentration $$n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\,\exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right)$$ where $N_c$, $N_v$ are effective density of states, $E_g$ band gap, $k$ Boltzmann constant, $T$ absolute temperature.

Extrinsic Semiconductor – semiconductor doped with donor ($N_D$) or acceptor ($N_A$) atoms.

  • n‑type: $N_D \gg N_A$, majority carriers electrons $n \approx N_D$, minority holes $p = \frac{n_i^2}{n}$.
  • p‑type: $N_A \gg N_D$, majority carriers holes $p \approx N_A$, minority electrons $n = \frac{n_i^2}{p}$.
  • Mass‑action law: $$n p = n_i^2$$
PropertyIntrinsicExtrinsic (n‑type)
Majority carrierBoth $n$ and $p$Electrons ($n \approx N_D$)
Minority carrierBoth $n$ and $p$Holes ($p = n_i^2 / N_D$)
Conductivity$\sigma = q (n_i \mu_n + n_i \mu_p)$$\sigma = q (N_D \mu_n + p \mu_p)$

SI Units

  • Carrier concentration: $\text{cm}^{-3}$ (or $\text{m}^{-3}$)
  • Mobility $\mu$: $\text{cm}^2\,\text{V}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}$
  • Conductivity $\sigma$: $\text{S}\,\text{m}^{-1}$

Example

Given $N_D = 10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$, $n_i = 1.5\times10^{10}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$ at $300\,$K, find electron concentration $n$ and hole concentration $p$.

  1. For an n‑type, $n \approx N_D = 10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$.
  2. Use mass‑action law: $p = \frac{n_i^2}{n} = \frac{(1.5\times10^{10})^2}{10^{16}} = 2.25\times10^{4}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$.
  3. Thus $\sigma = q (n \mu_n + p \mu_p)$. (Numerical substitution omitted for brevity.)
long_notes.Charge carriers, concentration and mobil:
Charge carriers – In an intrinsic semiconductor the charge carriers are electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band. Their concentrations are equal: $n = p = n_i$.

Carrier concentration

  • Intrinsic carrier concentration $n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\, e^{-E_g/(2kT)}$ (units: $\text{m}^{-3}$).
  • For an n‑type material $n \approx N_D$ and $p = \frac{n_i^2}{n}$.
  • For a p‑type material $p \approx N_A$ and $n = \frac{n_i^2}{p}$.

Mobility ($\mu$) – defined as the drift velocity per unit electric field:

$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E}$ (SI unit: $\text{m}^2\,\text{V}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}$).

Conductivity $\sigma$ is related to carrier concentration and mobility:

ParameterExpression
Electron contribution$\sigma_n = q n \mu_n$
Hole contribution$\sigma_p = q p \mu_p$
Total$\sigma = q\,(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)$

Example

At $300\,\text{K}$, silicon has $n_i = 1.5\times10^{16}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, $\mu_n = 0.14\,\text{m}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, $\mu_p = 0.05\,\text{m}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$. For an n‑type crystal doped with $N_D = 10^{22}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, find $\sigma$.

Solution: $n \approx N_D = 10^{22}$, $p = n_i^2/n = (1.5\times10^{16})^2/10^{22}=2.25\times10^{10}\,\text{m}^{-3}$. Then $\sigma = q (n\mu_n + p\mu_p) \approx 1.6\times10^{-19}(10^{22}\times0.14 + 2.25\times10^{10}\times0.05) \approx 2.24\times10^{2}\,\text{S m}^{-1}$.
long_notes.Energy band theory and carrier transport:
Energy Band Theory

  • Valence band (VB) – highest band completely filled with electrons at $T=0\\,\\text{K}$.
  • Conduction band (CB) – next higher band that is empty at $T=0\\,\\text{K}$.
  • Band gap $E_g$ – energy difference between the bottom of CB and top of VB. SI unit: joule (J) or electron‑volt (eV).
  • Intrinsic semiconductor – pure crystal; electron concentration $n$ equals hole concentration $p$, denoted $n_i$.

Carrier Concentration

QuantityExpressionSI Unit
Intrinsic carrier density$\\sqrt{N_c N_v}\\,\\exp\\left(-\\frac{E_g}{2kT}\\right)$m$^{-3}$
Electron concentration (n‑type)$n \approx N_D$ (for $N_D \\gg n_i$)m$^{-3}$
Hole concentration (p‑type)$p \approx N_A$ (for $N_A \\gg n_i$)m$^{-3}$

Transport Equations

  • Drift current density: $J_{drift}=q\\,\\mu\\,n\\,E$ (SI: A·m$^{-2}$).
  • Diffusion current density: $J_{diff}=q\\,D\\,\\frac{dn}{dx}$, where $D=\\mu\\,\\frac{kT}{q}$ (Einstein relation).

Example

Find the electron concentration $n$ in intrinsic Si at $300\\,\\text{K}$ given $n_i = 1.5\\times10^{10}\\,\\text{cm}^{-3}$.

  1. For an intrinsic material $n = p = n_i$.
  2. Convert to SI: $n = 1.5\\times10^{10}\\,\\text{cm}^{-3}\\times10^{6}=1.5\\times10^{16}\\,\\text{m}^{-3}$.
  3. Thus $n = 1.5\\times10^{16}\\,\\text{m}^{-3}$.

Key take‑aways: $E_g$ determines intrinsic carrier density; doping shifts $n$ or $p$ according to donor ($N_D$) or acceptor ($N_A$) concentration; drift and diffusion currents together describe carrier transport.
long_notes.Formation and properties of p‑n junction:
Definition: A p‑n junction is formed when a p‑type semiconductor (acceptor concentration $N_A$) is brought into intimate contact with an n‑type semiconductor (donor concentration $N_D$). Diffusion of majority carriers creates a depletion region that is free of mobile charge carriers.

Key results and formulas

  • Built‑in potential (contact potential): $V_{bi}=\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2}$ (unit: V).
  • Depletion width: $W=\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon_s}{q}\frac{N_A+N_D}{N_A N_D}V_{bi}}$ (unit: m).
  • Maximum electric field: $E_{max}=\frac{q N_D x_n}{\epsilon_s}=\frac{q N_A x_p}{\epsilon_s}$ (unit: V/m), where $x_n$ and $x_p$ are the n‑ and p‑side widths ($W=x_n+x_p$).

SI units

QuantitySymbolSI unit
Built‑in potential$V_{bi}$V
Depletion width$W$m
Electric field$E_{max}$V/m

Example

Calculate $V_{bi}$ for a silicon p‑n junction at $T=300\,\text{K}$ with $N_A=10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$, $N_D=10^{15}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$ and intrinsic carrier concentration $n_i=1.5\times10^{10}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$. Use $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\text{J/K}$ and $q=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

Solution: \[V_{bi}=\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2}=\frac{1.38\times10^{-23}\times300}{1.6\times10^{-19}}\ln\frac{10^{16}\times10^{15}}{(1.5\times10^{10})^2}\approx0.73\,\text{V}.\]

The built‑in potential of about $0.73\,\text{V}$ establishes the electric field that governs charge carrier motion across the junction.
long_notes.I‑V characteristics of p‑n junction diod:
Definition: A p‑n junction diode is a semiconductor device formed by joining p‑type and n‑type materials. Its I‑V characteristic shows exponential increase of current in forward bias and a very small leakage in reverse bias until breakdown.

Key formulas

  • Diode equation: $I=I_S\left(e^{\frac{qV}{n k T}}-1\right)$ where $I_S$ (A) is saturation current, $q=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$, $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\text{J K}^{-1}$, $T$ (K), $n\approx1$–2.
  • Small‑signal resistance: $r_d=\frac{n k T}{q I}$ (Ω).
  • Zener diode (reverse breakdown): $V_{Z}$ is the breakdown voltage, current obeys $I=I_S\left(e^{\frac{q(V+V_Z)}{n k T}}-1\right)$ for $V\approx -V_Z$.
  • LED forward voltage: $V_F\approx\frac{h c}{\lambda e}$ (V) where $\lambda$ is emission wavelength.
  • Photodiode current: $I=I_S\left(e^{\frac{qV}{n k T}}-1\right)-I_{ph}$, $I_{ph}$ (A) is photocurrent proportional to incident light.

SI Units: Current – ampere (A), Voltage – volt (V), Temperature – kelvin (K), Charge – coulomb (C).

Table: Typical parameters

DeviceBreakdown/Forward Voltage (V)Typical $I_S$ (A)
Zener$V_Z$ = 5.6 – 12$10^{-9}$ – $10^{-6}$
LED (red)$V_F$ ≈ 1.8 – 2.2$10^{-12}$ – $10^{-9}$
PhotodiodeReverse bias $\approx$ 5 – 20$10^{-12}$ – $10^{-9}$

Solved example

Given $I_S=10^{-12}\,\text{A}$, find the forward voltage $V$ for $I=1\,\text{mA}$ at $T=300\,\text{K}$ (assume $n=1$).

  1. Use diode equation rearranged: $V=\frac{n k T}{q}\ln\left(\frac{I}{I_S}+1\right)$.
  2. Thermal voltage $\frac{kT}{q}\approx25.85\,\text{mV}$.
  3. $\frac{I}{I_S}+1=\frac{10^{-3}}{10^{-12}}+1=10^{9}+1\approx10^{9}$.
  4. $V=25.85\,\text{mV}\times\ln(10^{9})=25.85\,\text{mV}\times20.72\approx0.535\,\text{V}$.

Thus the diode conducts at about $0.54\,\text{V}$ forward bias.
long_notes.Solar cell and its characteristics:
Solar cell (photovoltaic cell) is a p‑n junction device that directly converts incident photon energy into electrical energy via the internal photo‑electric effect.

Working principle

  • Photons with energy $h\nu \geq E_g$ generate electron‑hole pairs in the depletion region.
  • Built‑in electric field separates carriers, producing a photocurrent $I_{ph}$.
  • The cell behaves like a current source $I_{ph}$ in parallel with a diode characterized by saturation current $I_0$.

Current–voltage relation

$I = I_{ph} - I_0\left( e^{\frac{qV}{kT}}-1\right)$

From this, key parameters are derived:

  • Open‑circuit voltage: $V_{oc}=\frac{kT}{q}\ln\left(\frac{I_{ph}}{I_0}+1\right)$
  • Short‑circuit current: $I_{sc}=I_{ph}$ (when $V=0$)
  • Maximum power point: $P_{max}=V_{mp}I_{mp}$
  • Fill factor: $FF=\frac{V_{mp}I_{mp}}{V_{oc}I_{sc}}$
  • Efficiency: $\eta=\frac{P_{max}}{P_{\in}}\times100\%$, where $P_{\in}=G A$ (irradiance $G$ in W/m$^2$, area $A$ in m$^2$)

Typical characteristics

ParameterSymbolUnit
Open‑circuit voltage$V_{oc}$V
Short‑circuit current$I_{sc}$A
Maximum power$P_{max}$W
Fill factor$FF$—
Efficiency$\eta$%

Solved example

Given $I_{ph}=30\,\text{mA}$, $I_0=1\times10^{-12}\,\text{A}$, $T=300\,\text{K}$, find $V_{oc}$.

Constants: $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\text{J K}^{-1}$, $q=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Compute $\frac{kT}{q}=\frac{1.38\times10^{-23}\times300}{1.6\times10^{-19}}\approx0.02585\,\text{V}$. Ratio $\frac{I_{ph}}{I_0}=\frac{30\times10^{-3}}{1\times10^{-12}}=3\times10^{10}$. Hence $V_{oc}=0.02585\,\ln(3\times10^{10}+1)\approx0.02585\times24.12\approx0.62\,\text{V}$.

Thus the solar cell delivers an open‑circuit voltage of approximately $0.62\,\text{V}$ under the given conditions.
long_notes.Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT): opera:
Definition: A Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) is a three‑layer semiconductor device (NPN or PNP) in which current flow in the collector‑emitter circuit is controlled by a small base current.

Key Parameters:

  • $I_C$ – collector current (A)
  • $I_B$ – base current (A)
  • $I_E$ – emitter current (A)
  • $V_{BE}$ – base‑emitter voltage (V)
  • $V_{CE}$ – collector‑emitter voltage (V)
  • $\alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E}$ – common‑base current gain (unitless)
  • $\beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B}=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$ – common‑emitter current gain (unitless)

Fundamental Relations:

RelationExpression
Emitter current$I_E = I_C + I_B$
Collector current$I_C = \beta I_B$
Transconductance$g_m = \frac{\partial I_C}{\partial V_{BE}} = \frac{I_C}{V_T}$, $V_T \approx 26\,\text{mV}$ at 300\,K
Small‑signal emitter resistance$r_e = \frac{1}{g_m} = \frac{V_T}{I_E}$

Operating Regions:

  • Cut‑off: $I_B \approx 0$, $I_C \approx 0$.
  • Active (forward‑active): $V_{BE} \approx 0.7\,\text{V}$, $V_{CB}$ reverse‑biased, $I_C = \beta I_B$.
  • Saturation: $V_{CE} \le 0.2\,\text{V}$, both junctions forward‑biased.

Example:

Given $I_B = 20\,\mu\text{A}$, $\beta = 100$, $V_{CC}=10\,\text{V}$, $R_C=1\,\text{k}\Omega$, $R_E=500\,\Omega$.

Calculate:

  • $I_C = \beta I_B = 100 \times 20\,\mu\text{A} = 2\,\text{mA}$.
  • $I_E = I_C + I_B \approx 2.02\,\text{mA}$.
  • $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C - I_E R_E = 10 - (2\,\text{mA})(1\,\text{k}\Omega) - (2.02\,\text{mA})(500\,\Omega) \approx 5.99\,\text{V}$.

The transistor operates in the active region since $V_{CE} > 0.2\,\text{V}$.

long_notes.Concentration terms and units:
Solution: homogeneous mixture of solute & solvent.

  • Molarity (M): $M = \\frac{n_{solute}}{V_{solution}}$ (mol L$^{-1}$)
  • Molality (m): $m = \\frac{n_{solute}}{mass_{solvent\,(kg)}}$ (mol kg$^{-1}$)
  • Normality (N): $N = \\frac{equivalents}{V_{solution}}$ (eq L$^{-1}$)
  • Mass %: $\% w/w = \\frac{mass_{solute}}{mass_{solution}}\\times100$
  • Volume %: $\% v/v = \\frac{V_{solute}}{V_{solution}}\\times100$
  • ppm: $ppm = \\frac{mass_{solute}}{mass_{solution}}\\times10^{6}$
  • ppb: $ppb = \\frac{mass_{solute}}{mass_{solution}}\\times10^{9}$
  • Mole fraction (χ): $\\chi_{solute}= \\frac{n_{solute}}{n_{solute}+n_{solvent}}$

Key relation: For solutes where one mole provides $z$ equivalents, $N = M\\times z$.

TermFormulaSI Unit
Molarity$M = \\frac{n}{V}$mol L$^{-1}$
Molality$m = \\frac{n}{kg}$mol kg$^{-1}$
Normality$N = \\frac{eq}{V}$eq L$^{-1}$
Mass %$\% w/w = \\frac{m_{sol}}{m_{sol}+m_{solv}}\\times100$%
ppm$ppm = \\frac{m_{sol}}{m_{solution}}\\times10^{6}$mg L$^{-1}$ (approx)

Example: Find molarity of 58.5 g NaCl (M.W. = 58.5 g mol$^{-1}$) in 0.500 L solution.

Steps:

  1. $n = \\frac{58.5\,g}{58.5\,g\,mol^{-1}} = 1\,mol$
  2. $M = \\frac{n}{V} = \\frac{1\,mol}{0.500\,L} = 2.00\,M$

Thus the solution is $2.00\,M$ NaCl.
long_notes.Molarity, molarity calculations and solu:
Definition: Molarity ($M$) is the amount of solute (in moles) present per litre of solution.

SI unit: $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$ (often written as M).

  • Formula: $M = \frac{n\text{ (mol)}}{V\text{ (L)}}$ where $n$ is moles of solute and $V$ is volume of solution.
  • From mass: $n = \frac{m}{M_{r}}$ so $M = \frac{m}{M_{r}V}$ ($m$ = mass of solute, $M_{r}$ = molar mass).
  • Solution stoichiometry (dilution): $M_{1}V_{1}=M_{2}V_{2}$.
QuantitySymbolUnitExpression
Molarity$M$$\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$$M = \frac{n}{V}$
Moles$n$$\text{mol}$$n = \frac{m}{M_{r}}$
Mass$m$$\text{g}$$m = nM_{r}$

Example (Molarity calculation):

Find the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving $58.5\,\text{g}$ of NaCl ($M_{r}=58.44\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$) in $0.500\,\text{L}$ of water.

Step 1: $n = \frac{58.5}{58.44}=1.001\,\text{mol}$

Step 2: $M = \frac{1.001}{0.500}=2.00\,\text{M}$

The solution is $2.00\,\text{M}$ NaCl.
long_notes.Molality, normality and related concentr:
Molality (m) – amount of solute (in moles) per kilogram of solvent.

Formula: $\\frac{n_{solute}}{kg_{solvent}}$ → $m = \\frac{\\text{moles of solute}}{\\text{mass of solvent (kg)}}$.

SI unit: $\\text{mol·kg}^{-1}$.

Normality (N) – equivalents of solute per litre of solution.

One equivalent is the amount of substance that furnishes or consumes one mole of H⁺ or e⁻ in a reaction.

Formula: $N = \\frac{\\text{equivalents}}{\\text{volume of solution (L)}}$.

SI unit: $\\text{eq·L}^{-1}$.

Key relations

QuantityExpression
Molarity (M)$M = \\frac{n_{solute}}{V_{solution}}$ (mol·L$^{-1}$)
Normality (N)$N = M \\times n_{eq}$
Molality (m)$m = \\frac{M}{\\rho - M \\times M_{solvent}}$

Example

Calculate the molality of 58.5 g NaCl (M = 58.44 g·mol$^{-1}$) dissolved in 500 g water.

  • moles of NaCl = $\\frac{58.5}{58.44}=1.001\\text{ mol}$
  • mass of solvent = $0.500\\text{ kg}$
  • molality $m = \\frac{1.001}{0.500}=2.00\\text{ m}$
long_notes.Mole fraction, mole percent and related:
Definitions

  • Mole fraction (XA): $X_A = \\frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B + \dots}$ (dimensionless).
  • Mole percent (%A): $\\%_A = X_A \times 100$.
  • Mass fraction (wA): $w_A = \\frac{m_A}{m_{\\text{mix}}}$.

Key Relations

QuantityExpression
Mole fraction$X_A = \\frac{n_A}{\\sum n_i}$
Mole percent$\\%_A = X_A \times 100$
Mass fraction$w_A = \\frac{X_A M_A}{\\sum X_i M_i}$
Relation with molarity (M)$X_A = \\frac{M_A V}{\\sum M_i V_i}$ (for same volume)

SI Units

  • Mole fraction, mole percent, mass fraction – dimensionless (expressed in % for mole percent).
  • Molar mass $M$ – $\\text{kg mol}^{-1}$ (or $\\text{g mol}^{-1}$).

Example

In a binary mixture, $n_A = 2\\ \text{mol}$ and $n_B = 3\\ \text{mol}$. Find $X_A$, $\\%_A$ and $w_A$ if $M_A = 40\\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ and $M_B = 60\\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Solution:

  • $X_A = \\frac{2}{2+3} = \\frac{2}{5} = 0.40$.
  • $\\%_A = 0.40 \times 100 = 40\\%$.
  • Mass of A = $2 \times 40 = 80\\ \text{g}$, mass of B = $3 \times 60 = 180\\ \text{g}$, total mass = $260\\ \text{g}$.
  • $w_A = \\frac{80}{260} = 0.3077 \approx 30.8\\%$.

These expressions are frequently used in solution stoichiometry and colligative‑property calculations.
long_notes.Colligative properties – boiling point e:
Definition: A colligative property depends only on the number of solute particles in a given amount of solvent, not on their nature.

Key formulas:

  • Boiling‑point elevation: $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$
  • Freezing‑point depression: $\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m$
  • Molality: $m = \\frac{n_{solute}}{W_{solvent\,(kg)}}$

Symbols & SI units

SymbolMeaningUnit
$\Delta T_b,\ \Delta T_f$Change in boiling / freezing point$^\circ\mathrm{C}$
$i$Van’t Hoff factor (number of particles formed)dimensionless
$K_b,\ K_f$Boiling‑point / freezing‑point constant of the solvent$^\circ\mathrm{C\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$
$m$Molality of the solution$\mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$

Brief derivation (boiling‑point elevation)

At the boiling point the vapor pressure of the solution equals the external pressure. Adding a non‑volatile solute lowers the solvent’s vapor pressure by a factor $x_{solvent}$ (Raoult’s law). To restore the original vapor pressure the temperature must be raised, giving $\Delta T_b = iK_b m$.

Solved example

Calculate the boiling‑point elevation when $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of glucose ($i=1$) is dissolved in $500\ \mathrm{g}$ of water. $K_b$(water) $=0.512\ ^\circ\mathrm{C\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$.

Solution:

  1. Convert mass of water to kilograms: $W = 0.500\ \mathrm{kg}$.
  2. Molality $m = \\frac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.500\ \mathrm{kg}} = 2\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$.
  3. $\Delta T_b = i K_b m = 1 \times 0.512 \times 2 = 1.024\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
  4. New boiling point $= 100.00 + 1.024 = 101.024\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
long_notes.Vapor pressure lowering and Raoult’s law:
Vapor pressure lowering is the decrease in the equilibrium vapor pressure of a solvent when a non‑volatile solute is dissolved.

Raoult’s law (ideal solution) : $P_{\text{solution}} = X_{\text{solvent}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$

where $P_{\text{solution}}$ = vapor pressure of the solution, $X_{\text{solvent}}$ = mole fraction of solvent, $P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$ = vapor pressure of pure solvent (at same $T$).

Vapor‑pressure lowering, $\Delta P$, is obtained by subtracting the two pressures:

$$\Delta P = P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}} - P_{\text{solution}} = X_{\text{solute}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$$

Since $X_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solute}}+n_{\text{solvent}}}$, for dilute solutions $X_{\text{solute}}\approx\dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}$ and $\Delta P$ is directly proportional \to the amount of solute (a colligative property).

SymbolMeaningUnit
$P_{\text{solution}}$Vapor pressure of solutionPa or atm
$P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$Vapor pressure of pure solventPa or atm
$X_{\text{solvent}}$, $X_{\text{solute}}$Mole \frac{t}ions–
$\Delta P$Vapor‑pressure loweringPa or atm

Example : Calculate $\Delta P$ when 1 mol of a non‑volatile solute is dissolved \in 1 kg of water at $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($P^{\circ}_{\text{water}}=23.8\ \text{mmHg}$).

  • $n_{\text{solvent}} = \dfrac{1000\ \text{g}}{18\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 55.56\ \text{mol}$
  • $X_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{1}{1+55.56}=0.0177$
  • $\Delta P = 0.0177 \times 23.8 = 0.421\ \text{mmHg}$
  • $P_{\text{solution}} = 23.8 - 0.421 = 23.38\ \text{mmHg}$

Thus, the solution’s vapor pressure is lowered by $0.42\ \text{mmHg}$, illustrating Raoult’s law.
long_notes.Osmotic pressure and its applications:
Definition: Osmotic pressure ($\pi$) is the minimum pressure that must be applied on the solution side of a semipermeable membrane to stop the net flow of solvent from pure solvent to the solution.

Derivation (van’t Hoff): At equilibrium the chemical potentials of the solvent are equal: $\mu_1^{\text{pure}} = \mu_1^{\text{solution}} + V_1\pi$. Using $\mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln a$ and for a dilute solution $a \approx 1-\frac{n_2}{n_1}$, we obtain $\pi = iMRT$, where $i$ is the van’t Hoff factor.

SymbolMeaningUnit
$\pi$Osmotic pressurePa
$i$van’t Hoff factor–
$M$Molaritymol·L$^{-1}$
$R$Universal gas constant8.314 J·mol$^{-1}$·K$^{-1}$
$T$Absolute temperatureK

Key formula: $\pi = iMRT$ (SI: $\pi$ in Pa, $M$ in mol·m$^{-3}$, $T$ in K).

Units: 1 Pa = 1 N·m$^{-2}$; often expressed in atm (1 atm = $1.013\times10^5$ Pa).

Example: Calculate $\pi$ for a 0.10 mol·L$^{-1}$ glucose solution at $25^{\circ}$C (298 K). Glucose does not dissociate, so $i=1$.

Solution: $M = 0.10\,\text{mol·L}^{-1}=0.10\times10^{3}\,\text{mol·m}^{-3}=100\,\text{mol·m}^{-3}$. $\pi = iMRT = 1\times100\times8.314\times298 \approx 2.48\times10^{5}\,\text{Pa}=2.45\,\text{atm}$.
long_notes.Preparation of solutions and solution st:
Solution: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The component present in larger amount is the solvent and the other(s) are solutes.

Concentration terms (SI units)

TermFormulaUnit
Molarity (M)$M = \frac{n}{V}$mol L$^{-1}$
Molality (m)$m = \frac{n}{W_{solvent}}$mol kg$^{-1}$
Normality (N)$N = \frac{equivalents}{V}$eq L$^{-1}$
Mass % (w/w)$\% w/w = \frac{mass_{solute}}{mass_{solution}}\times100$%
Mole fraction (X)$X_{solute}=\frac{n_{solute}}{n_{total}}$dimensionless

Preparation of a solution

  • Weigh the required amount of solute.
  • Dissolve in a portion of solvent (usually water) in a beaker.
  • Transfer to a volumetric flask and make up to the mark with solvent.

Solution stoichiometry

  • For dilution: $C_1V_1 = C_2V_2$ where $C$ is concentration and $V$ is volume.
  • For reacting solutions: use $n = M\times V$ to find moles, then apply stoichiometric coefficients.

Example

Prepare $250\,\text{mL}$ of $0.2\,\text{M}$ NaCl solution.

  1. Calculate moles needed: $n = M\times V = 0.2\times0.250 = 0.050\,\text{mol}$.
  2. Mass of NaCl: $m = n\times M_{w}=0.050\times58.44 = 2.92\,\text{g}$.
  3. Weigh $2.92\,\text{g}$ NaCl, dissolve in about $150\,\text{mL}$ water, transfer to a $250\,\text{mL}$ volumetric flask and make up to the mark.

long_notes.Concentration terms and calculations:
Concentration Terms – Quick Reference

  • Molarity (M): $\\text{M}=\\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}}$, SI unit $\\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.
  • Molality (m): $\\text{m}=\\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solvent}}}$, SI unit $\\text{mol\,kg}^{-1}$.
  • Normality (N): $\\text{N}=\\frac{\text{equivalents}}{V_{\text{solution}}}$, $\\text{eq\,L}^{-1}$.
  • Mole fraction (X): $\\displaystyle X_{A}=\\frac{n_{A}}{\sum n_{i}}$ (dimensionless).
  • Mass percent (% w/w): $\\displaystyle \% w/w=\\frac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times100$.
  • Parts per million (ppm): $\\displaystyle \text{ppm}=\\frac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times10^{6}$.

Key Derivations

TermFormulaDerivation
Molarity$\\text{M}=\\frac{n}{V}$Number of moles $n=\frac{m}{M_{r}}$, $V$ in litres.
Molality$\\text{m}=\\frac{n}{m_{\text{solvent}}}$Mass of solvent $m_{\text{solvent}}$ in kg.
Normality$\\text{N}=\\frac{n\times\text{valency}}{V}$Equivalents = $n\times\text{valency}$.

Solved Example

Calculate the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving $58.5\,\text{g}$ of NaCl (M$_{r}=58.5\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$) in $500\,\text{mL}$ of water.

  1. Number of moles $n=\\frac{58.5}{58.5}=1\,\text{mol}$.
  2. Volume of solution $V=500\,\text{mL}=0.500\,\text{L}$.
  3. Molarity $M=\\frac{1}{0.500}=2.00\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Thus, the solution is $2.00\,\text{M}$ NaCl.
long_notes.Molarity, Molality and Normality:
Molarity (M) – number of moles of solute per litre of solution. $M = \frac{n}{V_{sol}}$ where $n$ is in mol and $V_{sol}$ in L. SI unit: mol·L$^{-1}$.

Molality (m) – moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. $m = \frac{n}{m_{solvent}}$. SI unit: mol·kg$^{-1}$.

Normality (N) – equivalents of solute per litre of solution. $N = \frac{eq}{V_{sol}} = \frac{n\times f}{V_{sol}}$, $f$ = equivalents per mole. SI unit: eq·L$^{-1}$.

Key relations

  • $M = \frac{N}{f}$
  • $m = \frac{M}{\rho - M\times M_{solute}}$ (approx., $\rho$ = density of solution in kg·L$^{-1}$)

Conversion table

QuantitySymbolFormula
Molarity$M$$M = \frac{n}{V_{sol}}$
Molality$m$$m = \frac{n}{m_{solvent}}$
Normality$N$$N = \frac{n\times f}{V_{sol}}$

Example: Prepare $250\,\text{mL}$ of $0.2\,\text{M}$ NaCl solution.

Required moles $n = M\times V = 0.2\times 0.250 = 0.050\,\text{mol}$. Mass $= n\times M_{NaCl}=0.050\times 58.44 = 2.92\,\text{g}$. We weigh $2.92\,\text{g}$ NaCl and dissolve in water and make up the volume to $250\,\text{mL}$.
long_notes.Mole fraction and mole percent:
Definition: The mole fraction of component $i$ in a mixture is the ratio of the amount of substance of that component to the total amount of substance.

$$X_i = \\frac{n_i}{\\sum_{j} n_j}$$

It is a dimension‑less quantity (SI unit: –).

Mole percent (mole %) is simply the mole \frac{t}ion expressed \in per cent:

$$\\text{Mole \%}_i = X_i \\times 100$$

Key relations

  • Mass \frac{t}ion $w_i = \\frac{m_i}{\\sum m_j}$.
  • Connecting $X_i$ and $w_i$: $$X_i = \\frac{w_i / M_i}{\\sum_{j} w_j / M_j}$$ where $M_i$ is molar mass (kg·mol$^{-1}$).

Typical values

Component$n$ (mol)$X_i$
Water2$\\frac{2}{5}=0.40$
Ethanol3$\\frac{3}{5}=0.60$

Example: A solution contains 2 mol of $\\mathrm{H_2O}$ and 3 mol of $\\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$. Find the mole \frac{t}ion and mole percent of water.

Solution: Total moles $n_{\\text{tot}} = 2 + 3 = 5$ mol.
$$X_{\\mathrm{H_2O}} = \\frac{2}{5} = 0.40$$
$$\\text{Mole \%}_{\\mathrm{H_2O}} = 0.40 \\times 100 = 40\%$$

Thus water constitutes 0.40 mole fraction or 40 % mole percent of the mixture.
long_notes.Colligative properties – boiling point e:
Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not on their nature. The two most important for Class‑12 are boiling‑point elevation ($\Delta T_b$) and freezing‑point depression ($\Delta T_f$).

Key definitions

  • Molality, $m = \frac{n_{solute}}{mass_{solvent}\;(kg)}$ (unit: mol·kg⁻¹).
  • Van’t Hoff factor, $i$, number of particles formed per formula unit (e.g., $i=2$ for NaCl).

Boiling‑point elevation

The rise in boiling point is given by

$\Delta T_b = K_b\,m$

where the ebullioscopic constant

$K_b = i\,\frac{R\,T_b^2}{\Delta H_{vap}}$

($R=8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}$, $T_b$ = normal boiling point in K, $\Delta H_{vap}$ = molar enthalpy of vaporisation in J·mol⁻¹). SI unit of $\Delta T_b$ and $K_b$ is kelvin (K).

Freezing‑point depression

The depression in freezing point is

$\Delta T_f = K_f\,m$

with the cryoscopic constant

$K_f = i\,\frac{R\,T_f^2}{\Delta H_{fus}}$

($T_f$ = normal freezing point, $\Delta H_{fus}$ = molar enthalpy of fusion). Units are identical to those of $K_b$.

Derivation (outline)

  • Start from Raoult’s law: $P_{solution}=x_{solvent}\,P^\circ_{solvent}$.
  • Equate chemical potentials of liquid and vapour at the new boiling/freezing point.
  • Replace mole fraction $x_{solvent}=\frac{1}{1+im}$ and linearise for dilute solutions ($im\ll1$).
  • Obtain $\Delta T = \frac{RT^2}{\Delta H}\,i m$, which defines $K_b$ or $K_f$.

Table of symbols

SymbolMeaningUnit
$\Delta T_b$Boiling‑point elevationK
$\Delta T_f$Freezing‑point depressionK
$K_b$Ebullioscopic constantK·kg·mol⁻¹
$K_f$Cryoscopic constantK·kg·mol⁻¹
$m$Molalitymol·kg⁻¹

Solved example

Calculate the boiling‑point elevation when 0.500 mol of a non‑volatile solute ($i=1$) is dissolved in 250 g of water. $K_b$(water) = 0.512 K·kg·mol⁻¹.

Molality: $m = \frac{0.500}{0.250}=2.00\;\text{mol·kg}^{-1}$.

Elevation: $\Delta T_b = K_b\,m = 0.512\times2.00 = 1.024\;\text{K}$.

New boiling point = $100.0\;\degree C + 1.024\;\text{K} \approx 101.0\;\degree C$.
long_notes.Vapor pressure lowering – Raoult’s law:
Vapor pressure lowering (Raoult’s law) – When a non‑volatile solute is dissolved in a volatile solvent, the vapour pressure of the solution ($P$) becomes lower than that of the pure solvent ($P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$). The decrease, $\Delta P$, is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the solute.

Key formula

  • $\Delta P = P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}-P = X_{\text{solute}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$
  • $P = X_{\text{solvent}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$ where $X_{\text{solvent}}=1-X_{\text{solute}}$

Derivation (outline)

  1. For an ideal solution, the escaping tendency of each component is proportional to its mole fraction.
  2. Hence $P_{\text{solvent}} = X_{\text{solvent}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$.
  3. Since $X_{\text{solvent}} = 1- X_{\text{solute}}$, substitute to obtain $\Delta P = X_{\text{solute}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$.

Symbols & SI units

SymbolMeaningUnit
$\Delta P$Vapour‑pressure loweringPa (or atm, mmHg)
$P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}$Vapour pressure of pure solventPa
$X_{\text{solute}}$Mole fraction of solutedimensionless

Solved example

Calculate the vapour‑pressure lowering when 1.00 mol of a non‑volatile solute is dissolved in 1.00 kg of water. $P^{\circ}_{\text{water}} = 23.8\,\text{mmHg}$ at 25 °C.

Number of moles of water $=\frac{1000\,\text{g}}{18.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}=55.5\,\text{mol}$.

Mole fraction of solute $X_{\text{solute}} = \frac{1.00}{1.00+55.5}=0.0177$.

Vapour‑pressure lowering $\Delta P = X_{\text{solute}}\,P^{\circ}_{\text{water}} = 0.0177\times23.8=0.42\,\text{mmHg}$.

New vapour pressure $P = 23.8-0.42 = 23.38\,\text{mmHg}$.

This illustrates the linear dependence of $\Delta P$ on the solute mole fraction as stated by Raoult’s law.
long_notes.Ideal and non‑ideal solutions:
Ideal Solution – a binary mixture that obeys Raoult’s law for the entire composition range. The mole fraction of component $i$ in the vapour phase $y_i$ equals its mole fraction in the liquid $x_i$ when the vapour behaves ideally.

Raoult’s law : $P=\sum_{i}x_iP_i^{*}$ where $P$ is the total vapour pressure (Pa) and $P_i^{*}$ is the vapour pressure of pure $i$ (Pa).

Non‑ideal Solution – shows deviation from Raoult’s law. Positive deviation ($P>\sum x_iP_i^{*}$) indicates weaker intermolecular forces; negative deviation indicates stronger forces.

  • Activity $a_i=\gamma_i x_i$, $\gamma_i$ being the activity coefficient (dimensionless).
  • Modified Raoult’s law: $P_i=\gamma_i x_i P_i^{*}$.
  • Relative volatility $\alpha_{AB}=\dfrac{K_A}{K_B}=\dfrac{\gamma_A P_A^{*}}{\gamma_B P_B^{*}}$.
  • Henry’s law for a dilute component: $P_i=k_H x_i$ (Pa, $k_H$ in Pa).
  • Excess Gibbs energy $G^{E}=RT\sum_{i}x_i\ln\gamma_i$ (J·mol$^{-1}$).
TermExpressionUnits
Partial pressure (ideal)$P_i=x_iP_i^{*}$Pa
Partial pressure (non‑ideal)$P_i=\gamma_i x_i P_i^{*}$Pa
Activity coefficient$\gamma_i=\dfrac{P_i}{x_iP_i^{*}}$–

Example: Calculate the total vapour pressure of an ideal binary solution containing 0.40 mol fraction ethanol ($P_{EtOH}^{*}=7.9\ \text{kPa}$) and 0.60 mol fraction water ($P_{H_2O}^{*}=3.2\ \text{kPa}$).

Solution: $P=0.40\times7.9+0.60\times3.2=3.16+1.92=5.08\ \text{kPa}$.

long_notes.Electrochemical cells and cell EMF:
Electrochemical Cell – A system where a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy.

Galvanic (Voltaic) Cell – Converts chemical energy → electrical energy; EMF $E_{\text{cell}} > 0$.

Electrolytic Cell – Uses external source to drive non‑spontaneous reaction; $E_{\text{cell}} < 0$.

Cell Notation – Example: $\text{Zn}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(a_{\text{Zn}^{2+}})||\text{Cu}^{2+}(a_{\text{Cu}^{2+}})|\text{Cu}$.

  • EMF (Cell Potential): $E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{cathode}} - E_{\text{anode}}$ (V).
  • Relation with Gibbs free energy: $\Delta G = -nF E_{\text{cell}}$.
  • Nernst Equation (general): $E = E^{\circ} - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$.
  • At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$: $E = E^{\circ} - \frac{0.0592}{n}\log Q$ (V).
  • Equilibrium constant: $\log K = \frac{nE^{\circ}}{0.0592}$.
  • For gases $Q = \frac{P_{\text{products}}^{\nu}}{P_{\text{reactants}}^{\nu}}$ (atm).
  • Temperature effect: $E$ decreases with increase in $T$ if $\Delta G > 0$.
Half‑reaction$E^{\circ}$ (V)
Zn$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$ → Zn$-0.76$
Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$ → Cu$+0.34$

Solved Example

Find $E_{\text{cell}}$ for $\text{Zn}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(0.010\,\text{M})||\text{Cu}^{2+}(1.0\,\text{M})|\text{Cu}$ at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Standard EMF: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\,\text{V}$.

Reaction quotient $Q = \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = \frac{0.010}{1.0}=0.010$.

Using Nernst equation: $E = 1.10 - \frac{0.0592}{2}\log(0.010) = 1.10 - 0.0296(-2) = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.1592\,\text{V} \approx 1.16\,\text{V}$.

SI Units: EMF – volt (V), concentration – mol·L$^{-1}$, pressure – atm, $F = 96\,485\,\text{C mol}^{-1}$.
long_notes.Standard electrode potential and Nernst:
Standard Electrode Potential (E°) – The emf of a cell when all its components are in their standard states (1 M, 1 atm, 25 °C). Unit: $\\text{V}$.

Nernst Equation – Relates cell potential at any condition to its standard potential:

$$E = E^{\\circ} - \\frac{RT}{nF}\\ln Q$$

  • $R = 8.314\\,\\text{J mol}^{-1}\\text{K}^{-1}$
  • $T$ – temperature \in $\\text{K}$
  • $n$ – number of moles of electrons transferred
  • $F = 96485\\,\\text{C mol}^{-1}$
  • $Q$ – reaction quotient

At $25\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C}$, $\\frac{RT}{F}=0.0257\\,\\text{V}$, and the equation is often written as:

$$E = E^{\\circ} - \\frac{0.0592}{n}\\log_{10} Q$$

SymbolMeaningUnit
$E$Cell potential$\\text{V}$
$E^{\\circ}$Standard cell potential$\\text{V}$
$Q$Reaction quotient–
$n$Electrons transferred–

Example: For the half‑reaction $\\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- -> Cu}$, $E^{\\circ}=+0.34\\,\\text{V}$. Calculate $E$ when $[\\ce{Cu^{2+}}]=0.010\\,\\text{M}$ at $25\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C}$.

Here $n=2$, $Q=\\frac{1}{[\\ce{Cu^{2+}}]}=\\frac{1}{0.010}=100$. Using the base‑10 form:

$$E = 0.34 - \\frac{0.0592}{2}\\log_{10} 100 = 0.34 - 0.0296\\times 2 = 0.34 - 0.0592 = 0.2808\\,\\text{V}$$

Thus the electrode potential drops \to $0.28\\,\\text{V}$ under the given conditions.
long_notes.Galvanic and electrolytic cells – cell n:
Definitions

  • Galvanic (voltaic) cell: Spontaneous redox reaction that produces electrical energy.
  • Electrolytic cell: Non‑spontaneous redox reaction driven by external emf.

Cell notation

General form: $\\text{anode (oxidation)}\\;|\\;\\text{oxidized species (aq)}\\;||\\;\\text{reduced species (aq)}\\;|\\;\\text{cathode (reduction)}$

ComponentSymbol
Anode (oxidation)$\\text{M}|\\text{M}^{n+}$
Cathode (reduction)$\\text{M}^{n+}|\\text{M}$
Salt bridge$||$

Cell potential

  • Standard cell emf: $E^{\\circ}_{\\text{cell}} = E^{\\circ}_{\\text{cathode}} - E^{\\circ}_{\\text{anode}}$ (unit: $\\text{V}$).
  • Nernst equation (25 °C): $E = E^{\\circ} - \\frac{0.0592}{n}\\log Q$, where $n$ = electrons transferred, $Q$ = reaction quotient.

Solved example

Find $E_{\\text{cell}}$ for the cell $\\text{Zn}|\\text{Zn}^{2+}(0.01\\,\\text{M})||\\text{Cu}^{2+}(1\\,\\text{M})|\\text{Cu}$.

  • $E^{\\circ}_{\\text{Cu}^{2+}/\\text{Cu}} = +0.34\\,\\text{V}$, $E^{\\circ}_{\\text{Zn}^{2+}/\\text{Zn}} = -0.76\\,\\text{V}$.
  • $E^{\\circ}_{\\text{cell}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\\,\\text{V}$.
  • $n = 2$, $Q = \\frac{[\\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = \\frac{0.01}{1}=0.01$.
  • $E = 1.10 - \\frac{0.0592}{2}\\log(0.01) = 1.10 - 0.0296(-2) = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.1592\\,\\text{V} \\approx 1.16\\,\\text{V}$.

Thus the galvanic cell delivers about $1.16\\,\\text{V}$ under the given conditions.
long_notes.Conductance of electrolytes, molar condu:
Conductance (G) and Conductivity (\kappa)

  • G = \frac{1}{R} \;(\text{S})
  • \kappa = \frac{G\,l}{A} \;(\text{S·cm}^{-1}) where l = distance between electrodes and A = cross‑sectional area.

Molar Conductivity (\Lambda_m) and Equivalent Conductivity (\Lambda_{eq})

  • \Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c} \;(\text{S·cm}^2\text{·mol}^{-1}) where c = molarity (mol·cm^{-3}).
  • \Lambda_{eq} = \frac{\kappa\,1000}{N} \;(\text{S·cm}^2\text{·eq}^{-1}) where N = normality.

Kohlrausch’s Law (Strong Electrolytes)

  • \Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{0} - K\sqrt{c}
  • \Lambda_m^{0}=\lambda_{+}^{0}+\lambda_{-}^{0} (sum of limiting ionic conductivities).

Units

  • \kappa: S·cm^{-1}
  • \Lambda_m: S·cm^{2}\text{·mol}^{-1}
  • \Lambda_{eq}: S·cm^{2}\text{·eq}^{-1}

Example

Determine the molar conductivity of 0.010 M NaCl solution. Cell constant $K=0.5\,\text{cm}^{-1}$, measured resistance $R=200\,\Omega$.

StepCalculation
1. Conductance$G=\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{200}=0.005\,\text{S}$
2. Conductivity$\kappa=G\times K=0.005\times0.5=0.0025\,\text{S·cm}^{-1}$
3. Molar conductivity$\Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa}{c}=\frac{0.0025}{0.010}=0.25\,\text{S·cm}^{2}\text{·mol}^{-1}$

Thus, $\Lambda_m=0.25\,\text{S·cm}^{2}\text{·mol}^{-1}$ for the given NaCl solution.

long_notes.Electrochemical cells and cell notation:
Electrochemical Cell – a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy (galvanic) or vice‑versa (electrolytic).

Cell notation represents the cell in a compact form:

ComponentSymbol
Anode (oxidation)$\text{Zn(s)}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(a)$
Cathode (reduction)$\text{Cu}^{2+}(a)|\text{Cu(s)}$
Salt bridge$||$

The general format is $\text{anode}|\text{anode\ ion\ (aq)}||\text{cathode\ ion\ (aq)}|\text{cathode}$.

  • Standard EMF: $E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}$ (V).
  • Nernst equation: $$E=E^\circ-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$$ where $n$ = electrons transferred, $F=96485\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$, $R=8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $T$ \in K.
  • At $298\ \text{K}$, $\frac{RT}{F}=0.0257\ \text{V}$, so $$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0257}{n}\ln Q$$.

Solved Example

Find $E_{cell}$ for the Daniell cell $\text{Zn(s)}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(0.010\ \text{M})||\text{Cu}^{2+}(0.10\ \text{M})|\text{Cu(s)}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. $E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}}=-0.76\ \text{V}$, $E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}}=+0.34\ \text{V}$.

Solution: $E^\circ_{cell}=0.34-(-0.76)=1.10\ \text{V}$. $Q=\frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}=\frac{0.010}{0.10}=0.10$. $n=2$. $$E=1.10-\frac{0.0257}{2}\ln(0.10)=1.10-0.01285\times(-2.302)=1.10+0.0296\approx1.13\ \text{V}$$.

Key points: EMF is positive for spontaneous galvanic cells; cell notation reads left to right (anode to cathode); the salt bridge maintains charge neutrality.
long_notes.Galvanic (voltaic) cells and EMF:
Galvanic (Voltaic) Cell – Definition
A galvanic cell is a spontaneous electrochemical system that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It consists of two half‑cells, each containing an electrode immersed in an electrolyte, connected by a salt bridge or porous membrane.

Cell Notation
General form: $\text{Zn(s)}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)\,||\,\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)|\text{Cu(s)}$ where “|” separates different phases and “||” denotes the salt bridge.

Key Formulas

  • Cell EMF (standard): $E^{\circ}_{cell}=E^{\circ}_{cathode}-E^{\circ}_{anode}$ (unit: V).
  • Nernst Equation (at $T$ K): $$E_{cell}=E^{\circ}_{cell}-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$$ where $R=8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $F=96485\,\text{C mol}^{-1}$, $n$ = electrons transferred, $Q$ = reaction quotient.
  • Relation with Gibbs free energy: $\Delta G=-nF E_{cell}$ (unit: J).

Units

  • EMF – volt (V)
  • Standard electrode potential – V
  • Gibbs free energy – joule (J)

Worked Example

Calculate the EMF of the cell $\text{Zn(s)}|\text{Zn}^{2+}(1.0\,\text{M})||\text{Cu}^{2+}(0.10\,\text{M})|\text{Cu(s)}$ at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$.

  1. Standard potentials: $E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}}=+0.34\,\text{V}$, $E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}}=-0.76\,\text{V}$.
  2. $E^{\circ}_{cell}=0.34-(-0.76)=1.10\,\text{V}$.
  3. Reaction: $\text{Zn(s)}+\text{Cu}^{2+}\rightarrow\text{Zn}^{2+}+\text{Cu(s)}$, $n=2$.
  4. Reaction quotient $Q=\frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}=\frac{1.0}{0.10}=10$.
  5. At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, $\frac{RT}{F}=0.0257\,\text{V}$, so $$E_{cell}=1.10-\frac{0.0257}{2}\ln 10=1.10-0.0296=1.07\,\text{V}.$$

Thus, the cell EMF is $1.07\,\text{V}$, confirming the spontaneous nature of the reaction.

long_notes.Introduction to chemical kinetics:
Chemical Kinetics – Introduction

Chemical kinetics studies the speed at which reactants are converted to products and the factors influencing this speed.

Key Definitions

  • Rate of reaction = change in concentration per unit time, $r = -\\frac{1}{\\nu_i}\\frac{d[A_i]}{dt}$.
  • Rate law expresses $r$ in terms of concentrations of reactants: $r = k\\, [A]^m [B]^n$.
  • Order of reaction = sum of exponents $m+n$; determines the dependence on concentration.
  • Rate constant ($k$) – proportionality factor; its SI unit varies: $\\text{s}^{-1}$ for first order, $\\text{M}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$ for second order.
  • Half‑life ($t_{1/2}$) – time for concentration to fall to half its initial value.

Important Integrated Forms

OrderIntegrated Rate LawHalf‑life
Zero$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$
First$\\ln\\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{\\ln 2}{k}$
Second$\\frac{1}{[A]} - \\frac{1}{[A]_0}=kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$

Sample Problem (First‑order decomposition)

For the reaction $N_2O_5 \rightarrow 2NO_2 + \\frac{1}{2}O_2$, $[N_2O_5]$ falls from $0.10\\,\\text{M}$ to $0.025\\,\\text{M}$ in $30\\,\\text{min}$. Find $k$ and $t_{1/2}$.

Solution:

Using the first‑order law $\\ln\\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt$:

$k = \\frac{1}{30}\\,\\ln\\frac{0.10}{0.025}=\\frac{1}{30}\\,\\ln 4 = \\frac{\\ln 4}{30}\\,\\text{min}^{-1}=0.0462\\,\\text{min}^{-1}$.

Half‑life $t_{1/2}=\\frac{\\ln 2}{k}=\\frac{0.693}{0.0462}=15\\,\\text{min}$.

Thus $k=0.046\\,\\text{min}^{-1}$ and $t_{1/2}=15\\,\\text{min}$.
